claims.claim: Jenny Turner's 2001 LRB essay dismisses Tolkien's prose style in passing without analysis.
claims.source: Jenny Turner 2001, as reported in Curry, 'The Critical Response to Tolkien's Fiction'
claims.quote: dreadful prose style

claims.claim: The reader's impression of archaicity comes partly from over-use of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and rare or obsolescent words.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation into The Lord of the Rings' (CL2017)
claims.quote: three simple lexical causes

claims.claim: Keywords shared with nineteenth-century novels cluster in landscape, position/direction (whither, thither, thence, yonder, afar), warfare, and descriptive verbs/adjectives, many obsolete when Tolkien wrote.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: so many of the keywords used to describe its settings

claims.claim: Tolkien borrows words such as valour, valiant and corslet from his Beowulf translation and stretches them beyond their Old and Middle English range.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: Tolkien borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf

claims.feature: modern words in old grammatical patterns
claims.claim: Even core modern words are used in nineteenth-century patterns, e.g. 'a black smoke' with the indefinite article, rare in modern fiction.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: tends to use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns

claims.claim: Tolkien follows a modernist tendency in his abundant manner-laden verbs: clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, glimmer, loom, peer, plod, stride, twist.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: abundant use of descriptive verbs

claims.claim: Words key only to Tolkien (dingle, fen, glades, starless, lore-masters, wolf-riders, yesteryear, yuledays, along/among/outwards) are rare but not archaic and together create otherworldliness.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: an atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness

claims.claim: Tolkien prefers the most homely collocations available yet uses everyday adjectives like 'great' in unusual pairings, and his key semantic domains (speed, size, loudness) point to hyperbole.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: a marked preference for the most homely collocations available

claims.claim: Far from amateurish, the prose deploys several centuries of linguistic development, putting old words to new uses and vice versa.
claims.source: Siepmann CL2017
claims.quote: he is a linguistic postmodernist

claims.claim: Keyword, n-gram and collocation methods show the style of The Lord of the Rings relies heavily on nineteenth-century novels and on Tolkien's Beowulf translation.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a Stylist: Key Words and Key Collocations' (2021), ch. 2
claims.quote: relies heavily on the nineteenth-century novel

claims.claim: The full subtlety of Tolkien's collocations has escaped both casual readers and literary critics.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 2
claims.quote: escaped both the casual reader's and the literary critic's notice

claims.claim: The third-person narrator presents the point of view of a group of characters, usually hobbits, recorded in ordinary language.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 4 'Points of View'
claims.quote: usually hobbits

claims.claim: Other passages carry an archaic diction reminiscent of ancient epic and Macpherson's Ossian, conveying an omniscient point of view tied to epic characters like Aragorn.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 4
claims.quote: archaic diction, reminiscent of ancient epic poetry

claims.claim: Limiting point of view to certain characters' perceptions, thoughts and feelings follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 4
claims.quote: follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice

claims.claim: Thomas calls the narrator of The Lord of the Rings self-effacing, unintrusive and vanishing, and counts ten different viewpoints in the opening chapter.
claims.source: Paul Edmund Thomas, 'Some of Tolkien's Narrators' (2000), as quoted in Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 4
claims.quote: ten different viewpoints

claims.claim: The Hobbit opens with a very intrusive narrator who recedes as the book grows serious; by The Lord of the Rings the narrator is impartial and multi-viewpoint, measured on Wayne Booth's scale.
claims.source: Thomas 2000, as summarised in kate_nepveu's reading notes
claims.quote: impartial and self-effacing

claims.claim: In The Hobbit fairy-tale and epic discourses are set against everyday speech through irony and parody.
claims.source: Thomas Kullmann, 'Intertextual Patterns in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings', NJES 8(2) 2009 (abstract via Semantic Scholar API)
claims.quote: juxtaposed with everyday speech through irony and parody

claims.claim: In The Lord of the Rings nineteenth-century circumstantial realism and pathetic fallacy combine with archaic rhetorical patterns.
claims.source: Kullmann 2009 (abstract)
claims.quote: circumstantial realism and pathetic fallacy combine with archaic rhetorical patterns

claims.claim: The Aragorn/Boromir/Elrond exchange is a quieter English, extraordinary for simple timelessness, with sobriety, wit and force — the language of men of character.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973)
claims.quote: It has sobriety, wit, and force

claims.claim: Tolkien writes a plain, clear English whose outstanding virtue is flexibility and variety, from the commonplace to the stately.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately

claims.claim: Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking; everything is direct, concrete and simple, with no 'ichor'.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking; he has no ichor

claims.claim: The prose can slide into metrical poetry, as in the Bombadil episode, without careless readers noticing.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: can slide into metrical poetry

claims.claim: The archaic manner is a perfect distancer but a high wire on which one slip spoils all; Eddison did it perfectly, novices fake it with -est and mayhap.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: The archaic manner is indeed a perfect distancer

claims.claim: Alternating colloquial American for humour and old formal usage for earnest moments (Leiber, Zelazny) jerks the reader between Elfland and Poughkeepsie and breaks character coherence.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: the characters lose coherence in my mind

claims.claim: The journalistic plainness of bad fantasy is flat not simple, inexact not clear, with vague sensory cues; Tolkien's plainness is the real thing.
claims.source: Le Guin 1973
claims.quote: is not really simple, but flat

claims.claim: The rhythm shaping the narrative is stress/release, a walking gait, carried without faltering across the whole book.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), quoted in kate_nepveu's reading notes
claims.quote: as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats

claims.claim: 'Fog on the Barrow-downs' pulses between polarities — darkness/daylight, confusion/clarity, trap/freedom — and each pole grows out of its opposite.
claims.source: Le Guin 2001, via kate_nepveu
claims.quote: a pulsation back and forth between polarities

claims.claim: The chapter's closing sentences reverse darkness/lights, downhill/up, hill/village, fire/night in quiet simple language, like drumbeats.
claims.source: Le Guin 2001, via kate_nepveu
claims.quote: They are like drumbeats

claims.claim: On the irreducible simplicity of the trochaic beat Tolkien builds a complex, stable rhythmic pattern in imagined space and time.
claims.source: Le Guin 2001, via kate_nepveu (Google Books confirms 'trochaic' on p. 106 of The Wave in the Mind)
claims.quote: Relying on the irreducible simplicity of the trochaic beat

claims.claim: Even long sentences follow the breath, punctuation falls where one needs to pause, and the cadences are graceful and inevitable.
claims.source: Le Guin, quoted in Jason Fisher, 'Reading The Lord of the Rings aloud' (Lingwë, 2010)
claims.quote: the cadences are graceful and inevitable

claims.claim: In Middle-earth one can hardly put a foot down without stirring the dust of history; the world is heavy with past.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, 'The Gods Return to Earth' (Time and Tide, 1954), reproduced at TheOneRing.com
claims.quote: without stirring the dust of history

claims.claim: The invented names alone are a feast.
claims.source: Lewis 1954
claims.quote: The names alone are a feast

claims.claim: The book marks the unashamed return of gorgeous, eloquent heroic romance in an anti-romantic age.
claims.source: Lewis 1954
claims.quote: heroic romance, gorgeous, eloquent, and unashamed

claims.claim: No other prose writer has captured the piercing, high, elvish beauty Tolkien achieves.
claims.source: Lewis 1954
claims.quote: piercing, high, elvish beauty

claims.claim: Keeping the reader aware of parallel story-lines adds immensely to pathos, irony and grandeur.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, 'The Dethronement of Power' (1955), via kate_nepveu's reading notes
claims.quote: adds immensely to the pathos, irony, and grandeur

claims.claim: The first chapter is a little shy-making, but once the story moves the initial archness disappears.
claims.source: W. H. Auden, 'The Hero Is a Hobbit' (NYT, 1954), excerpted at Epistle of Dude
claims.quote: this initial archness disappears

claims.claim: Tolkien possesses an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description.
claims.source: Auden 1954
claims.quote: a wonderfully exact eye for description

claims.claim: By the end one knows the histories of Hobbits, Elves, Dwarves and their landscape as well as one's own childhood.
claims.source: Auden 1954
claims.quote: as well as one knows one's own childhood

claims.claim: The hobbits closely resemble the arcadian rustics of British detective fiction.
claims.source: Auden 1954
claims.quote: those arcadian rustics

claims.claim: The language of portal-quest fantasy is elaborate in the anthropologist's or pre-Raphaelite painter's way, intensely descriptive and exploratory.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), Introduction
claims.quote: the elaboration of the anthropologist or the pre-Raphaelite painter

claims.feature: reader positioned at a point of entry
claims.claim: Mendlesohn treats The Lord of the Rings as portal-quest rhetoric in which the reader learns the world from a point of entry, the process traced in her chapter one.
claims.source: Mendlesohn 2008, Introduction
claims.quote: we learn from a point of entry

claims.claim: Descriptions sound vividly detailed but give an open-ended outline the reader fills in, so readers feel they helped make the world.
claims.source: Steve Walker, interview on The Power of Tolkien's Prose (Tolkien Library)
claims.quote: invitational quality

claims.claim: Scholars missed Tolkien's style because sentence-level style is not on the sociological critic's radar, though it mattered greatly to Tolkien.
claims.source: Walker interview
claims.quote: isn't on our scholarly radar

claims.claim: Like a folk mythology the legendarium comes in many forms, with multiple versions in differing styles and levels of detail (Bratman's Estate essay does not name the four modes attributed to him elsewhere).
claims.source: David Bratman, 'The History of Middle-earth' (Tolkien Estate)
claims.quote: multiple versions in differing styles and levels of detail

claims.claim: Olsen's close reading tracks changes in tone as The Hobbit's stakes grow and distinguishes High Elves from Mirkwood elves through their speech.
claims.source: David Oberhelman, Mythopoeic Society review of Corey Olsen, Exploring J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit
claims.quote: changes in tone as the stakes become greater

claims.claim: Mythgard's Exploring The Lord of the Rings is an explicitly sentence-level reading, but no transcripts or notes are published; only titles are public.
claims.source: Mythgard Institute, Exploring the Lord of the Rings project page
claims.quote: sentence by sentence

claims.claim: The Council of Elrond succeeds by representing many tongues, with Gandalf performing the voice of each speaker he reports, from Saruman to the Gaffer and Butterbur.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, 'Could The Council of Elrond Have Been an Email?'
claims.quote: of polyglossia

claims.claim: Art is the achievement of expression that gives a Secondary World the inner consistency of reality; consistency, not novelty, is what earns belief.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories' (full text, coolcalvary PDF)
claims.quote: the inner consistency of reality

claims.feature: Secondary Belief vs suspension of disbelief
claims.claim: Inside a successful Secondary World what is related is 'true' by that world's own laws, and the instant a reader's disbelief arises the art has failed — suspension of disbelief is only a substitute for genuine Secondary Belief.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: The moment disbelief arises, the spell is broken

claims.claim: Fantasy's native advantage is arresting strangeness, which must be married to consistency or it decays into the merely fanciful and decorative.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: arresting strangeness

claims.claim: The more the images depart from the Primary World the harder inner consistency is to produce, so fantastic material demands more labour than sober material, not less.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: easier to produce this kind of “reality” with more “sober” material

claims.claim: Anyone can say 'the green sun'; building a world in which it commands Secondary Belief requires labour, thought and a special elvish craft — narrative art in its most potent mode.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: a kind of elvish craft

claims.claim: The adjective is the root spell of Faërie: to take green from grass or red from blood is already an enchanter's power, so fantasy is built at the level of the word.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: a part of speech in a mythical grammar

claims.claim: Fantasy's function of Recovery is regaining a clear view, freeing familiar things from the triteness of appropriation — the prose must make the known strange again.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: the drab blur of triteness or familiarity

claims.feature: fantasy belongs to words, not pictures or drama
claims.claim: Fantasy is best left to words because painting makes the fantastic technically too easy and Drama is naturally hostile to Fantasy — the verbal medium is the proper one.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: Fantasy is a thing best left to words

claims.claim: Faërie is indescribable though not imperceptible; the writer gives glimpses rather than definitions, and analysis will not discover the secret of the whole.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: cannot be caught in a net of words

claims.claim: The association of fairy-stories with children is a historical accident, so the register must not be pitched down to a nursery audience.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: an accident of our domestic history

claims.claim: The fairy-story's true form is the sudden joyous turn that denies universal defeat without denying sorrow, so the prose must carry grief and joy in one register.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: poignant as grief

claims.claim: A fairy-story must be presented as true and cannot tolerate any frame or machinery suggesting the whole is a figment or illusion.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'On Fairy-Stories'
claims.quote: presented as 'true'

claims.claim: The instinct of linguistic invention is the fitting of notion to oral symbol and pleasure in contemplating the relation — words must sound like what they mean.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice' (full text, gwern PDF)
claims.quote: the fitting of notion to oral symbol

claims.claim: Pleasure in articulate sound and its symbolic use is independent of communication though entangled with it, and must never be forgotten in language-making.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: pleasure in articulate sound

claims.claim: An invented language with individual flavour must have a mythology woven into it, and conversely language construction will breed a mythology — names and tongue come first, the world grows to fit.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: your language construction will breed a mythology

claims.claim: Tolkien's chief interest is word-form in itself and word-form in relation to meaning, the so-called phonetic fitness.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: word-form in relation to meaning

claims.feature: verse as the test of an invented language
claims.claim: The final fruition of an invented language is verse, which both expresses and fixes the maker's personal taste in sound.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: this final fruition: verse

claims.claim: In modern poetry word-form is seldom consciously marked and its effects are miscalled 'authentic magic'; Tolkien wants sound-pattern deliberately constructed to give pleasure.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: the word-form is seldom consciously marked

claims.claim: Word-form even unassociated with notions can give a perception of beauty; Greek, Finnish and Welsh are named as languages with characteristically beautiful word-form.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: capable of giving pleasure - a perception of beauty

claims.feature: association of form and sense (cellar door)
claims.claim: 'Cellar door' is beautiful dissociated from its sense, and the higher pleasure lies in words where form and sense associate — a phonaesthetic test the prose can be held to.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Cellar door' (quoting 'English and Welsh')
claims.quote: the association of form and sense

claims.claim: Linguistic taste is partly inborn (the 'native tongue' as distinct from the cradle-tongue), so a writer's phonaesthetic choices express inherent predilections rather than fashion.
claims.source: Anna Smol, 'Tolkien's cellar door' (quoting 'English and Welsh' pp.190-1)
claims.quote: inherent linguistic predilections

claims.feature: illusion of historical truth and perspective
claims.claim: The illusion of historical truth and perspective in Beowulf is largely a product of art — an instinctive historical sense used with a poetical, not historical, object.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' (full text PDF)
claims.quote: largely a product of art

claims.claim: The impression of depth is the effect and justification of episodes and allusions to old tales that are darker and more desperate than the foreground — the background must be grimmer than the story.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: mostly darker, more pagan, and desperate than the foreground

claims.claim: Old stones (sources) exist to build the tower from whose top one sees the sea; the work is art, not a quarry, and its sources must not be dug for at the tower's expense.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: look out upon the sea

claims.claim: The poem's structure is a balance, an opposition of ends and beginnings (youth against age), not a steadily advancing narrative.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: an opposition of ends and beginnings

claims.claim: Old English lines are founded on a balance of two opposed halves, more like masonry than music, and the whole is a composition not a tune.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: more like masonry than music

claims.claim: Beowulf is not an epic but an heroic-elegiac poem whose first 3,136 lines are the prelude to a dirge — the elegiac is the governing tone.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: the prelude to a dirge

claims.feature: late, antiquarian voice (echo of an echo)
claims.claim: The poem is late not primitive: its maker told of things already old and weighted with regret, producing sorrows both poignant and remote.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: an echo of an echo

claims.claim: A translation must avoid colloquialism and false modernity and be literary and traditional, because the original's diction was poetical, archaic and artificial in its own day.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'On Translating Beowulf'
claims.quote: colloquialism and false modernity

claims.claim: The language should be intentionally antiquated but not arcane — words still in literary use among educated people — avoiding both the colloquial and the obscure.
claims.source: Philip Irving Mitchell (DBU), outline of 'On Translating Beowulf'
claims.quote: avoid both the colloquial and the obscure

claims.claim: The translator owes allegiance to the original's meaning and style and renders it into modern literary English, not present-day colloquial English.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, J.R.R. Tolkien 'Thoughts on Translation (Beowulf)'
claims.quote: modern literary, not present-day colloquial

claims.claim: Resolving Old English compounds into phrases keeps colour but loosens and weakens the texture; compact naming is preferred.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'On Translating Beowulf'
claims.quote: loosens and weakens the texture

claims.claim: Publishing The Hobbit under the convention that fairy-stories are for children had unfortunate effects on its mode of expression and narrative method, which he would have corrected if not rushed.
claims.source: Carpenter (ed.), The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 215 to Walter Allen (April 1959, unsent draft)
claims.quote: unfortunate effects on the mode of expression and narrative method

claims.claim: Intelligent children of good taste single out the points in manner where the address is to children as blemishes.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 215'
claims.quote: singled out the places where the address was to children

claims.feature: whimsy to historical (register arc of The Hobbit)
claims.claim: The Hobbit begins in a whimsy, even facetious, mode and moves steadily to a more serious, consistent and historical one — and he regrets much of the early manner.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 215
claims.quote: more consistent and historical

claims.feature: LotR addressed to no class of reader
claims.claim: The Lord of the Rings was not specially addressed to children or any other class but to anyone who enjoys a long exciting story; adult language is assumed.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 215
claims.quote: a long exciting story

claims.claim: In so far as The Hobbit was dressed up as for children in style or manner, Tolkien regrets it, and so, he says, do the children.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 165 to Houghton Mifflin (June 1955)
claims.quote: in style or manner, I regret it

claims.claim: Words like plenilune and argent are beautiful before they are understood; limiting vocabulary to a child's supposed reach cuts off the gifted from extending it.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 234 to Jane Neave (22 Nov 1961)
claims.quote: beautiful words before they are understood

claims.feature: first meeting in a living context
claims.claim: A fine word should first be met in a living context, not a dictionary; 'argent' does not mean 'silver' because its phonetic incarnation and heraldic overtones differ.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 234
claims.quote: in a living context, and not in a dictionary

claims.claim: Tolkien deprecated the writing-down, flattening attitude that leaves children with little respect and no love for words; The Hobbit's early part was his one such mistake.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 234'
claims.quote: writing down, flattening attitude

claims.claim: The Lord of the Rings is meant to include, even in style, the colloquialism and vulgarity of hobbits, poetry, and the highest style of prose.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 131 to Milton Waldman (1951)
claims.quote: the colloquialism and vulgarity of Hobbits

claims.feature: tone rises with the hero's development
claims.claim: In The Hobbit the tone and style change with the hobbit's development, passing from fairy-tale to the noble and high and relapsing on the return.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 131
claims.quote: passing from fairy-tale to the noble and high

claims.claim: The legendarium ranges from the cosmogonic to the fairy-story level, the larger founded on the lesser and the lesser drawing splendour from the vast backcloths.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Letter 131)
claims.quote: the lesser drawing splendour from the vast backcloths

claims.claim: Westron is equated with English and everything in it translated with differentiation of style for dialect; related tongues become English-related forms (Rohan like Old English, Dale Scandinavian); alien tongues are left alone.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144 to Naomi Mitchison (25 Apr 1954)
claims.quote: some differentiation of style to represent dialectal differences

claims.claim: In Gondor the Common Speech is spoken in a nobler and more antique style, which the Elves also adopt when they use it.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144
claims.quote: nobler and rather more antique style

claims.claim: As a story it is good that many things stay unexplained (especially if an explanation exists); Tolkien fears he erred by explaining too much, and readers stuck at the Council of Elrond.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144
claims.quote: a lot of things unexplained

claims.claim: Quenya is built on a Latin basis with Finnish and Greek because they give him phonaesthetic pleasure; Sindarin is devised to resemble British-Welsh because that character fits Celtic-type legends.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144
claims.quote: give me ‘phonaesthetic’ pleasure

claims.claim: The invention of languages is the foundation, the stories were made to provide a world for the languages, a name comes first and the story follows, and the book is largely an essay in linguistic aesthetic.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 165
claims.quote: largely an essay in ‘linguistic aesthetic’

claims.claim: Only as much 'language' was left in The Lord of the Rings as readers could be expected to stomach — the visible Elvish is a deliberate restraint.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 165
claims.quote: as I thought would be stomached by readers

claims.claim: The sensibility to linguistic pattern affects Tolkien emotionally like colour or music; Gothic taught him aesthetic pleasure in a language for its own sake.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 163 to W.H. Auden (7 Jun 1955)
claims.quote: affects me emotionally like colour or music

claims.claim: A tale of this sort must consult the writer's roots: a man of the North-west sets it in a world with the Shoreless Sea to the West and endless enemy lands to the East.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 163
claims.quote: consult your roots

claims.claim: Tushery is bogus medieval stuff coloured with expletives like tush, pish, zounds; real archaic English is far terser than modern and says things the slack modern idiom cannot.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171 to Hugh Brogan (Sept 1955, unsent draft)
claims.quote: far more terse than modern

claims.claim: Putting Théoden's thought into modern idiom would be an insincerity, a disunion of word and meaning, because people who think like that do not talk a modern idiom.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171
claims.quote: a disunion of word and meaning

claims.claim: Narrative (not only dialogue) archaism is defended because heroic scenes do not occur in a modern setting; changing the idiom would be like changing helms and hauberks into modern uniforms.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171
claims.quote: helms, shields, hauberks into modern uniforms

claims.claim: 'Helms too they chose' puts the emphasised word in prominent first place without a clutter of empty words, a trick modern English should relearn by example.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171
claims.quote: a lot of little ‘empty’ words

claims.claim: English's wealth leaves a choice of styles without any risk of unintelligibility, and refusing to use it is a parochialism of time.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171
claims.quote: a choice of styles

claims.feature: Elrond's archaism by grammar and vocabulary
claims.claim: The Gateway summary of the Brogan draft records Tolkien rejecting 'tushery' as applying only to low-quality pastiche rather than real archaic English, with the Théoden passage as his sample.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 171'
claims.quote: slack and often frivolous idiom

claims.feature: legends and language share a taste
claims.claim: Legends depend on the language they belong to and a living language on its legends; Esperanto is dead for lack of legends, and Tolkien's legends were invented to match his languages' taste.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 180 to 'Mr Thompson' (14 Jan 1956)
claims.quote: legends of the same ‘taste’

claims.feature: differentiation by diction and idiom, not accent
claims.claim: No vowel/consonant accent-marking is wanted; Orcs deliberately never drop aitches in the text; the linguistic differentiation Tolkien built is in diction and idiom.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 193 to Terence Tiller (2 Nov 1956)
claims.quote: in diction, idiom, and so on

claims.feature: Minas Tirith as the standard register
claims.claim: Minas Tirith is to the Common Speech as London is to modern English — the standard of comparison, whose people have no accent.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 193
claims.quote: as London is to modern English

claims.claim: The Rohirrim spoke with a slower tempo and more sonorous articulation than modern urbans, and in Common Speech speak the best Minas Tirith, perhaps a little too carefully as a learned tongue.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 193
claims.quote: a slower tempo and more sonorous articulation

claims.feature: Orcs nasty by delivery not vulgarism
claims.claim: Orcs are to sound nasty through intonation, articulation and tempo, not through conventional features of modern vulgar English.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 193'
claims.quote: intonation, articulation, and tempo

claims.feature: reading, not drama (necklace on a thread)
claims.claim: The book needs the older art of the reading mime; dramatization flattens scenery and characters, whereas passages read as a necklace upon a thread of narration would be fairer.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 194 to Terence Tiller (6 Nov 1956)
claims.quote: as a necklace upon a thread of narration

claims.claim: The tale was conceived epically rather than dramatically, so dramatizing it without liberties strips setting from dialogue and leaves both flat.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 194'
claims.quote: a tale told epically

claims.feature: verse triggers archaic style; no modern rusticity
claims.claim: A speaker who breaks into formal verse uses an archaic style as anyone capable of verse then would; where dialect marked place not rank, avoid any modern rusticity.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 152 to Rayner Heppenstall (22 Sept 1954)
claims.quote: avoid any modern rusticity

claims.feature: miles are miles (literal geography and season)
claims.claim: Though a fairy-story, the tale takes place in this earth's northern hemisphere: miles, days and weather are literal, and seasons are pictorial and basic to the tone.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210 to Forrest J. Ackerman (June 1958)
claims.quote: miles are miles, days are days, and weather is weather

claims.feature: tone not to be lowered to childish fairy-tale
claims.claim: 'Old scamp!' exemplifies the treatment's tendency to lower the tone toward a childish fairy-tale; the setting is not fairy-land but real river-lands in autumn.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: in real river-lands in autumn

claims.feature: neither contes de fées nor scientification
claims.claim: Any pull toward French fairy-tale style or toward science-fiction diction ('food concentrate' for lembas) is alien to the story; both modes are rejected.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: Both modes are alien to my story

claims.feature: characters kept in style and sentiment
claims.claim: Speeches must represent the characters as written, in style and sentiment; perverting a character is resented more than spoiling plot or scenery.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: in style and sentiment

claims.claim: Anticipating later devices and assimilating one incident to another have a flattening effect; a scene of gloom and silence beats yet another scene of screams and slashings.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: flattening the tale out

claims.claim: The Ringbearers' action and the heroic matter are totally different in tone and scenery and must each be kept in coherent sequence; jumbling destroys both.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: totally different in tone and scenery

claims.claim: Rohan is a dwelling of Men in a heroic age: no private chambers, the king receiving on the dais of his hall — details must fit the world described.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: a dwelling of Men in an ‘heroic age’

claims.claim: Gandalf must not splutter: despite humour and an avuncular manner he is a person of high and noble authority and great dignity.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 210'
claims.quote: Gandalf was to be spluttering. Tolkien disapproved

claims.feature: a world for the languages (personal aesthetic)
claims.claim: The long book was an attempt to create a world for languages that agreed with his personal aesthetic — a situation in which an Elvish greeting would be ordinary.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 205'
claims.quote: create a world for languages

claims.feature: glimpses of a large history; unattainable vistas
claims.claim: Part of the attraction is the glimpses of a large history in the background, like a distant city in sunlit mist; to go there destroys the magic unless new unattainable vistas open.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 247 to Colonel Worskett (20 Sept 1963)
claims.quote: unless new unattainable vistas are again revealed

claims.feature: language requires a habitation and history
claims.claim: Anyone who carries language invention far discovers that a language requires a suitable habitation and a history in which it can develop — the origin of the imaginary histories.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 294 to the Plimmers (8 Feb 1967)
claims.quote: a suitable habitation, and a history

claims.claim: The nomenclature, built from pre-existing invented languages, achieves a verisimilitude that assists literary belief in the story as historical; name-meanings are relevant solely to the fiction.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 297 drafts to 'Mr Rang' (Aug 1967)
claims.quote: the ‘literary belief in the story as historical

claims.feature: Anglo-Saxon as translation device for Rohan only
claims.claim: Anglo-Saxon is used for the Mark's names and glimpses of its speech purely as a device of translation, and is the sole field for those names — delusory anywhere else.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 297
claims.quote: as a device of ‘translation’

claims.claim: Tolkien objected to translating personal nomenclature and insisted the word hobbit stay unaltered; the Shire is a parody of rural England whose toponymy is not Dutch.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 190'
claims.quote: the word hobbit stayed unaltered

claims.claim: Shire names are not meaningless but English in form, built from elements now obsolete, dialectal, or worn-down and obscured.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings' (Nomenclature, full text)
claims.quote: obsolete or dialectal

claims.feature: euphonious names of familiar English style
claims.claim: Common-Speech renderings of Elvish names (Rivendell for Imladris) are made to be both a translation and a euphonious name of familiar English style.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: a euphonious name of familiar English style

claims.claim: Leaving such names untranslated would introduce an unexplained element with no place in the feigned linguistic history of the period — the nomenclature is a single designed scheme.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: the feigned linguistic history of the period

claims.feature: hobbits adopt the style of those they meet
claims.claim: Appendix F explains varied hobbit speech by saying the more learned hobbits knew book-language and were quick to adopt the style of those they met.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (quoting Appendix F)
claims.quote: quick to note and adopt the style

claims.feature: Appendix F cut to a third
claims.claim: The published Appendix F is only about one-third as long as its draft F2 — the visible linguistic apparatus is a deliberate reduction.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'The Appendix on Languages'
claims.quote: only about one-third as long

claims.claim: Scholars summarise the depth effect as four techniques: enormous background scale, casual incomplete mentions, multiple accounts with apparent contradictions (Red Book frame), and varying literary styles.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: casual, incomplete mentions

claims.feature: editorial frame (last of the philological editors)
claims.claim: Tolkien positioned himself as the last of a line of philological editors of the Red Book, so the paratexts make the text seem annotated by many hands over ages.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's frame stories'
claims.quote: the last of a line of philological editors

claims.claim: In the Valedictory Address Tolkien says he would rather wring the juice out of a single sentence or explore one word than survey — the sentence-level craft is the method.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Tom Shippey on 'The Monsters and the Critics and other essays'
claims.quote: wring the juice out of a single sentence

claims.claim: Tolkien singularised the speech of important characters to show social and cultural differences and asked why one should refuse to use the wealth of English.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Ferré, Lauzon and Riggs, 'Translating Tolkien'
claims.quote: refuse to use the wealth of English

claims.claim: To give a language individual flavour it must have woven into it the threads of an individual mythology.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Carl Hostetter, 'Tolkien's Invented Languages'
claims.quote: the threads of an individual mythology

claims.claim: The incarnate mind, the tongue and the tale are coeval; sub-creation is a birthright because we make as we are made.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Verlyn Flieger, 'On Fairy Stories'
claims.quote: We make, because we are made

claims.claim: The Lord of the Rings shows far more deliberate stylistic variation than any other novel, with sixty poems and songs in many styles and several languages.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Tom Shippey, 'The Lord of the Rings, Book of the Century'
claims.quote: far more deliberate stylistic variation

claims.claim: A reader's essay argues Elrond's age is implied by archaic word order and that each character's speech stays consistent throughout, conveying culture and rank.
claims.source: K.G., 'To Make a Soul: Tolkien and Variations of Speech' (tolkienmedievalandmodern blog)
claims.quote: Elrond's age and sagacity implied through archaic word order

claims.claim: Moorcock holds that high fantasy's prose is the prose of the nursery-room, a lullaby meant to soothe, and that this is the predominant tone of The Lord of the Rings — the direct counter to Tolkien's claim to have shed the children's manner.
claims.source: Michael Moorcock, 'Epic Pooh' (1978; revolutionsf copy via Wayback)
claims.quote: the prose of the nursery-room

claims.claim: Bratman and Williams reject Moorcock's reading of the prose as out of context and uninformed.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Epic Pooh'
claims.quote: one wonders what book Moorcock read

claims.claim: Kullmann states on p. 111 that 85 per cent of the non-direct-speech (narrative) sections follow the point-of-view conventions of the nineteenth-century novel, i.e. are told from a hobbit's limited point of view.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: 85 per cent, of the non-direct-speech sections of the narrative

claims.claim: Wikipedia's sentence that the narrative is told '85% of the time' from one of the four hobbits' viewpoints is footnoted to Kullmann & Siepmann 2021 pp. 90-122; the figure itself sits on p. 111 of the 'Points of View' chapter.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: 85% of the time

claims.claim: Holmes reports that Kullmann measures the dominance of the hobbit point of view as 85% of all non-direct speech representing hobbits, and that the hobbits are the foci of 'psychonarration' (p. 105).
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)
claims.quote: 85% of all “non-direct” speech

claims.claim: Kullmann finds about 50 per cent of the text is dialogue, exclamations, embedded stories and recited poems, whereas in a novel direct speech would usually take up about 20 to 30 per cent (p. 90; repeated at p. 159).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: usually take up ca. 20 to 30 per cent

claims.claim: Wikipedia summarises K&S: about half of the novel is dialogue, poetry and song or embedded stories, against roughly 25% dialogue in a typical modern novel.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Bolding's review reports Kullmann's finding that direct speech comprises 50 percent of the text (K&S p. 90), with narrative oversight from the hobbits' point of view while keeping the third person.
claims.source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: using direct speech to comprise 50 percent of the text

claims.claim: Turner notes Kullmann's point that the proportion of direct speech is higher than usual in nineteenth- or twentieth-century novels because it serves purposes beyond social conversation and evokes older pre-texts.
claims.source: Allan Turner, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Inklings Studies 12.1 (2022)

claims.claim: Omniscient narration is comparatively rare; the reader is most commonly given the point of view of a group of characters, usually hobbits, before it narrows to an individual (p. 90).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: omniscient narration is comparatively rare

claims.claim: The 'Points of View' chapter abstract: the narrator mostly presents the point of view of hobbits as a group or of Frodo, Sam, Pippin or Merry, and only to a far lesser extent Aragorn, Gimli, Legolas and Éowyn.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'Points of View' (ch. 4) abstract, Springer
claims.quote: to a far lesser extent Aragorn, Gimli, Legolas and Éowyn

claims.feature: ordinary language for hobbit viewpoint vs archaic omniscient passages
claims.claim: Hobbits' points of view are recorded in ordinary language, while other passages use an archaic diction reminiscent of ancient epic and Macpherson's Ossian and convey an omniscient point of view tied to 'epic characters' like Aragorn.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'Points of View' (ch. 4) abstract, Springer
claims.quote: recorded in “ordinary” language

claims.claim: Tolkien's limited point of view follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice; Kullmann traces the technique from Walpole's Castle of Otranto (1764) through Pride and Prejudice, Waverley, The Mill on the Floss, Tess, Mary Webb and Buchan's Witch Wood (p. 92).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: Emphasis is laid on subjective experience rather than facts

claims.claim: Like Scott's Waverley and Buchan's David Sempill, the hobbits act as intermediaries and, in Turner's phrase quoted by Kullmann, as representatives of the normality of the reader in a strange environment (pp. 95, 123).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: Tolkien's hobbits act as intermediaries

claims.feature: mediation as the function of limited POV
claims.claim: The function of the point-of-view technique is mediation: a strange environment and chain of events is brought close to the reader through the intermediate agency of characters whose point of view is recorded; the technique goes back to historical fiction (p. 119).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: brought close to the reader through the intermediate agency

claims.claim: The narrator does not explain why an event has occurred; explanation is left to other characters such as Gandalf or Aragorn, or to the hobbits' own subjective conclusions (p. 91).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: left to other characters, such as Gandalf or Aragorn

claims.claim: Psychonarration (Lanser's term) is reserved to Frodo; what Gandalf thinks or plans is left to Frodo's and the reader's speculation (p. 105).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: Psychonarration is reserved to Frodo

claims.claim: Gandalf speaks a lot but his thoughts and feelings are hardly ever communicated to the reader in third-person narration (p. 118).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: hardly ever communicated to the reader

claims.claim: When Aragorn's viewpoint is used we are told what he sees but learn little of his thoughts and feelings (p. 114); an omniscient passage gives way to a hobbit-limited one to lend Aragorn psychological depth via Merry's gaze (p. 102).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: we do not learn much about his thoughts and feelings

claims.claim: The narrative function of Merry and Pippin is to let the novelist take a hobbit's point of view on each spreading strand of the plot after Frodo and Sam leave the Company at the end of Book 2 (p. 99).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: a hobbit's point of view to each of the spreading strands

claims.feature: focaliser shift from Frodo to Sam
claims.claim: In the first two books Frodo observes the world; later Frodo becomes the object of Sam's gaze, with Sam the focalizer in Books 4 and 6 (pp. 108, 119).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: the object of Sam's gaze

claims.feature: limited POV raises tension and characterises
claims.claim: As in nineteenth-century novels, the limited point of view both characterises a person and raises tension; Frodo's viewpoint conveys what he is barely conscious of, e.g. 'finding' he has put on the Ring (p. 105).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.claim: Sections told by an omniscient narrator are comparatively few, and some (the Prologue, the accounts of Bree and Minas Tirith) resemble a different text type, eighteenth-century antiquarianism such as Percy's Reliques (p. 111).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: comparatively few in number

claims.claim: The 'epic style' first seen with the Riders of Rohan recurs particularly at moments when a battle's outcome is imminent: Helm's Deep, the siege of Gondor, and when the Ring falls into the Cracks of Doom (p. 113).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: at moments when the outcome of a battle is imminent

claims.claim: The epic passages' short sentences, parataxis, inversion and repetition, with darkness and night motifs, are reminiscent of Macpherson's Poems of Ossian (p. 116).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: short sentences, parataxis, inversion and repetition

claims.claim: In the Rohirrim passages sentences follow one another paratactically, more complex propositions are built with participles, there are few hypotactic sentences, and the effort of the journey is conveyed by inversions (p. 115).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: there are few hypotactical sentences

claims.claim: Kullmann inverts Lubbock/Friedman: the omniscient archaic passages are the vivid visual 'showing', while point-of-view passages mainly serve to show states of mind rather than to describe action (p. 120).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: mainly serve to show certain states of mind

claims.claim: Kullmann notes the shift from Genette's focalisation externe to focalisation interne on Frodo, who becomes Bal's 'focalisé' or Lanser's 'focalizer', but he prefers the historical term 'point of view' (p. 123).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: Frodo becomes the “focalisé”

claims.feature: hobbit viewpoint vs archaic speech registers
claims.claim: The archaic register of Dwarves and Men contrasts starkly with the language of the hobbits and of the narrator, who usually tells the story from the hobbits' points of view (p. 217).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: usually tells the story from the hobbits' points of view

claims.claim: Turner: Kullmann's psychonarration, events filtered through an individual's limited point of view, is typical of the realistic novel; where no hobbits are present the focus on 'archaic' characters brings narrative language of an older epic tradition.
claims.source: Allan Turner, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Inklings Studies 12.1 (2022)

claims.claim: Turner: K&S dispel any notion of one 'Tolkien style', showing skilful use of several styles resonating with the last few hundred years of English writing.
claims.source: Allan Turner, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Inklings Studies 12.1 (2022)
claims.quote: dispel any notion that there is any one ‘Tolkien style’

claims.feature: parataxis vs hypotaxis as cultural registers
claims.claim: Bolding reports Kullmann's contrast of parataxis and hypotaxis as defining the Rohirrim and Gondor cultures, with Gandalf the one speaker who moves fluidly between social registers.
claims.source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: his contrast of parataxis and hypotaxis

claims.claim: Bolding summarises ch. 9: Gandalf and Frodo are the most flexible speakers, Sam undergoes the most evolution, Gimli and Legolas keep the most traditional registers, Merry and Pippin use common English as reality-based touchstones.
claims.source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: Gandalf and Frodo are found to be the most flexible

claims.claim: Holmes cites K&S data that Aragorn opens future pronouncements with 'shall' half again as often as Gandalf and seven times as often as Sam or Pippin.
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)
claims.quote: seven times as often as Sam or Pippin

claims.claim: Holmes: K&S's data tend to refute the long-held view of the prevalence and significance of archaic inversions in Tolkien (K&S p. 40).
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)
claims.quote: the prevalence and significance of archaic inversions

claims.claim: Holmes: Kullmann identifies 45 to 50 intercalated stories told by twenty-three characters, in three categories (simultaneous events, exposition, mythological past); Bolding gives 23 storytellers.
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)
claims.quote: 45 to 50 “intercalated” stories told by twenty-three characters

claims.claim: Siepmann's syntax chapter uses a corpus separating dialogue from narrative, with the PHRASEOROM post-war fiction corpus and the BNC as references, extracting the most significant 3- to 6-grams of syntactic tags and attending to constructions Tolkien avoids as well as prefers.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'The Narrative Syntax of The Lord of the Rings' (ch. 3) abstract, Springer
claims.quote: constructions that Tolkien, compared to other authors, tends to avoid

claims.claim: Siepmann finds that the short copular sentences and modal 'would' uses that signal free indirect speech in modern fiction are conspicuous by their absence from The Lord of the Rings (pp. 75-76).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: conspicuous by their absence from The Lord of the Rings

claims.feature: inner monologue rendered by omniscient narrator
claims.claim: Short sentences of the kind found in modern fiction tend to be direct renditions by an omniscient narrator of characters' inner monologue, a strategy Tolkien does not use (p. 75).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: direct renditions by an omniscient narrator of characters' inner monologue

claims.claim: Instead of free indirect thought Tolkien overuses clauses reporting a character's thoughts with a that-clause ('He thought that he had heard a faint voice') and 'It seemed that' constructions (p. 84).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: It seemed that he had made some decision

claims.claim: At clause level the first thing to note is an evident underuse of personal pronouns in sentence-initial position, against the contemporary-fiction patterns 'She longed to say it', 'He had expected to fight' (p. 74).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: underuse of personal pronouns in sentence-initial position

claims.claim: Pronoun reference is a dispreferred strategy; given the unusually large cast, reference by name becomes a frequent necessity (p. 75).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: reference by name becomes a frequent necessity

claims.claim: At word level Tolkien underuses modal verbs relative to post-war fiction (p. 72).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: underuse of modal verbs

claims.claim: Clause-initial participle clauses introduced by an adverb and followed by a main clause ('Already cringing ..., she suddenly felt') are comparatively rare in The Lord of the Rings (p. 75).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.claim: The most conspicuous clause-level idiosyncrasy is the fronting of adverbials, as in 'to a (N) they came' (p. 78).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: the fronting of adverbials

claims.claim: Tolkien overuses 'then', 'presently' and 'suddenly' in clause-initial position (p. 78).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: overuse of then, presently or suddenly in clause-initial position

claims.claim: Even a casual reader notices Tolkien's fondness for inverted constructions, most commonly fronted subject complements followed by copular be and the subject ('beautiful was its colour'), and fronted prepositional phrases with other verbs (p. 81).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: fronted subject complements followed by copular be and the subject

claims.claim: Turner notes Siepmann distinguishes linguistically between inversion and fronting whereas Kullmann uses 'inversion' for both in the rhetorical sense.
claims.source: Allan Turner, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Inklings Studies 12.1 (2022)
claims.quote: between inversion and fronting

claims.claim: An overused clause variant is a passive verb followed by a prepositional complement ('Her shield was shivered in many pieces'), with passive slots filled by original or obsolescent material; the stative passive is far more common than the eventive (pp. 79-80, 83).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: the stative passive is far more common than the eventive

claims.claim: Tolkien, unlike many novelists, clearly prefers clause-initial over clause-final participial clauses, sometimes reduced to a bare absolute participle ('he, bowing low to the fallen, bade them'), though participial constructions are generally underused (p. 80).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: clear preference for clause-initial participial clauses

claims.claim: Tolkien uses existential clauses with a wide variety of verbs to describe events ('there came ...'), fronted prepositional phrases with existential there, and existential there with passives ('there was held the highest feast'), but hardly ever for mere presence or absence (pp. 76, 82-83).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: existential clauses with a wide variety of verbs

claims.claim: Clauses and phrases coordinated by 'and' feature prominently; Tolkien uses 'and' with high frequency but sometimes differently from other writers (Table 3.1 'Use of and'; pp. 76, 86).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: Clauses and phrases coordinated by and feature prominently

claims.claim: Dialogue-framing sentences of the type 'said Frodo' (verb before name) are a recurrent feature of the narrative syntax (pp. 84-85).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: dialogue-framing sentences (said Frodo)

claims.claim: Sentence-initial 'at last' combined with a short verb, and fronted adjectives functioning as subject complements, are typical sentence openers (p. 84).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.claim: Key verbs shared with modern fiction are highly descriptive (clutch, cower, crawl, flicker, gape, gasp, gaze, gleam), while Tolkien overuses the emphasizers very, so and too and the adverb 'even', about seven times more common than in modern fiction (pp. 47, 49, 59).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: around seven times more common than in modern fiction

claims.claim: The first half of the book is less densely descriptive; tight clusters of high descriptivity peak in Book Four, chapters II and VII (p. 48).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: three outstanding peaks in Book Four

claims.claim: Siepmann's 2017 corpus study: the impression of archaicity comes from overuse of nineteenth-century fiction words (yonder, journey (v), topmost), avoidance of modern-world words, and dense use of coinages, unusual patterns and obsolescent words; reference corpora were 30m (19th-c fiction), 160m (post-war fiction) and 94m (mixed).
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation' (Corpus Linguistics 2017, Birmingham)
claims.quote: three simple lexical causes

claims.claim: Modern key words (they, big, wake, wall, tired, smoke) are used in nineteenth-century patterns, e.g. 'a black smoke' with indefinite article, rare in modern fiction.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation' (Corpus Linguistics 2017, Birmingham)

claims.claim: Wikipedia cites Turner: Tolkien's style is generally simple parataxis, varied by the race and standing of the speaker; at Pelennor the paratactic repeated 'and' creates an exalted biblical register with few archaic words.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style
claims.quote: repeated use of 'and'

claims.claim: Wikipedia cites Shippey's 'loose semantic fit' (conjunctions avoiding explicit logical connection) at significant moments and Rosebury on inversion working better than the plain order ('But glad would he have been').
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style

claims.claim: McIntosh, citing Garth (p. 271), describes Tolkien's parataxis as short simple sentences joined by 'and' in the Ride of the Rohirrim and Pelennor, producing breathless excitement and rising foreboding.
claims.source: Jonathan McIntosh, 'Tolkien's use of parataxis', The Flame Imperishable (2012)
claims.quote: sense of breathless excitement

claims.claim: Thomas (per Nepveu): The Hobbit opens with a very intrusive narrator who recedes as the book grows serious; the LOTR narrator is impartial and self-effacing, and early LOTR drafts were unsuccessful returns to the intrusive voice (Booth's scale).
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, summary of Paul Edmund Thomas, 'Some of Tolkien's Narrators' (2000)
claims.quote: impartial and self-effacing

claims.claim: Poveda: The Hobbit's narrator is omniscient, comments on events, addresses the reader as a child, withholds and anticipates information, and is conscious of the written medium.
claims.source: Jaume Albero Poveda, 'Narrative models in Tolkien's stories of Middle-earth', Journal of English Studies 4 (2003-04)

claims.claim: Poveda: LOTR begins in a conversational tone with Hobbit-style asides and an occasionally unreliable narrator ('probably started by the knowledgeable Sam'), but as the plot progresses the voice becomes neutral and the narrator disappears behind the characters.
claims.source: Jaume Albero Poveda, 'Narrative models in Tolkien's stories of Middle-earth', Journal of English Studies 4 (2003-04)
claims.quote: the narrator disappears behind the characters

claims.feature: archaic style confined to elf/men episodes
claims.claim: Poveda: archaic forms (ye, hath) and noun-adjective inversion are not predominant but confined to episodes of Elves and Men inspired by epic, chiefly Books II and III; capitalised common nouns (the Sea, the City) mark the style.
claims.source: Jaume Albero Poveda, 'Narrative models in Tolkien's stories of Middle-earth', Journal of English Studies 4 (2003-04)
claims.quote: chiefly books II and III

claims.claim: Litschko, using Stanzel and Booth, characterises The Hobbit's narrator as an intrusive authorial narrator who comments and judges, addresses readers directly, shifts point of view, and changes tone in the later-written final chapters.
claims.source: Nadja Litschko, 'The Voice of the Narrator in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit' (GRIN, 2006)
claims.quote: intrusive authorial narrator

claims.feature: limited omniscience when no hobbit present
claims.claim: aefenglommung: the story is seen mainly through Frodo's mind, occasionally Merry or Pippin, and increasingly Sam; where no hobbit is present Tolkien draws back into limited omniscience and we do not enter Aragorn's, Gimli's or Legolas's minds, Book 3 reading like a stage-play.
claims.source: aefenglommung, 'Point of view in LOTR' (LiveJournal, 2021)
claims.quote: we do not enter their minds

claims.feature: multiple tellers and limited vs omniscient narrators
claims.claim: Barkley compares the versions of tales told by Bilbo, Aragorn, Gandalf, the Red Book's scholar-editor and the Silmarillion's omniscient narrator: the limited narrator is narrower in scope but richer in detail, dialogue and song, the omniscient broader in theme.
claims.source: Christine Barkley, 'Point of View in Tolkien', Mythlore 21.2 (1996)
claims.quote: The limited third-person narrative focuses attention more on one character

claims.claim: Barkley: the Prologue's Red Book of Westmarch frame authenticates the tale, gives away the happy ending, and contrasts with The Hobbit, whose narrator paraphrased Bilbo's account and revealed his own bias.
claims.source: Christine Barkley, 'Point of View in Tolkien', Mythlore 21.2 (1996)

claims.claim: Wikipedia cites Thomson (1967) and Turner (2011) for the found-manuscript frame in which Tolkien poses as editor/translator of the Red Book, with genealogies and footnotes as editorial apparatus.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Tauber: The Hobbit's 19 chapters (70th Anniversary edition) yield 95,137 whitespace tokens in 11,532 types, or 95,390/95,643 depending on em-dash handling; 5,165 types carry trailing punctuation and 254 contain em-dashes.
claims.source: James Tauber, 'Tokenizing the Hobbit' (Digital Tolkien Project, 2021)
claims.quote: 95,137 tokens in 11,532 types

claims.claim: Tauber: The Hobbit has 1,566 paragraphs; 85.8% are uniquely identifiable by their first three tokens and 98.5% by five or fewer.
claims.source: James Tauber, 'Minimal Prefixes to Identify Hobbit Paragraphs' (Digital Tolkien Project, 2021)

claims.claim: Tauber: in LOTR a single-sentence utterance followed by a tag ends in a comma before the closing quote; 'A,' said X, 'B.' versus 'A,' said X. 'B.' distinguish one interrupted sentence from two, and the first form is ambiguous.
claims.source: James Tauber, 'Punctuation and Structure in Marking Up Direct Speech' (Digital Tolkien Project, 2019)

claims.claim: The Digital Tolkien Project reports speaker identification completed for The Hobbit, The Lord of the Rings and The Silmarillion, enabling dialogue/narrative separation by speaker.
claims.source: Digital Tolkien Project, Overview and Sub-Projects
claims.quote: Speaker identification has been completed

claims.claim: Tauber's Oxonmoot 2023 abstract applies Multidimensional Register Analysis across The Book of Lost Tales, The Hobbit, LOTR and The Silmarillion, asking whether the Silmarillion's elevated style appears in Elven direct speech in LOTR, noting these shifts had not previously been studied quantitatively.
claims.source: Digital Tolkien Project, 'Upcoming Talks' (2023) with Oxonmoot abstract 'Linguistic Variation in Tolkien's Writing Styles'
claims.quote: have not previously been studied quantitatively

claims.claim: Rateliff collates counts: LotR Project 481,103; an unofficial count 478,492 without appendices and 526,172 with; The Hobbit 95,356; The Silmarillion 130,115; Tolkien's own 1950 estimate was 600,000.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, 'Just How Long is LotR Anyway? (word counts)', Sacnoth's Scriptorium (2017)

claims.claim: Livesey's corpus: The Hobbit 95,559 tokens; the two books of The Two Towers 66,374 and 64,738 tokens; 'ring' occurs 306 times in Fellowship (1.72 per thousand words), 70 in Two Towers (0.45) and 73 in Return of the King.
claims.source: Michael Livesey, 'The Ring Cycle: Journeying Through the Language of Tolkien's Third Age with Corpus Linguistics', JTR 18.1 (2023)
claims.quote: a total wordcount of 95,559 tokens

claims.claim: Beasley's chapter-level corpus of The Hobbit (19 chapters) and LOTR (5 prologue sections plus 61 chapters) totals 578,432 tokens.
claims.source: Michael H. Beasley, 'A Spatial Text Analysis of J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-Earth' (USC senior thesis, 2019)
claims.quote: the total word count calculated, was 578,432

claims.claim: Shugar's grammatical analysis of The Hobbit's opening finds an average sentence length of 19 words, a longest sentence of 59 words, nested clauses with coordinating conjunctions and em-dash interruptions.
claims.source: Amelia Shugar, 'A Grammatical Journey down the Hobbit Hole' (2019)
claims.quote: an average sentence length of 19 words

claims.claim: Forum counting finds a 144-word sentence in the original Fall of Gondolin tale, cites an online claim that the longest LOTR sentence is 111 words, and corrects a 96-word count to 97; Tolkien's punctuation is credited with keeping such sentences readable.
claims.source: The Tolkien Forum thread 'Tolkien's Longest Sentence?' (2022)
claims.quote: one long sentence, counting at 144 words

claims.claim: Qiu extracts The Hobbit's dialogue by regex on text enclosed in double quotation marks across 19 chapters; top dialogue words are good (89), time (65), Baggins (46).
claims.source: Lilin Qiu, 'Quantifying Emotional Tone in Tolkien's The Hobbit' (arXiv 2512.10865, 2025)
claims.quote: text enclosed in double quotation marks

claims.claim: LotrProject reports The Hobbit has more unique words and a higher unique-word density than The Silmarillion and each LOTR volume (2009 HarperCollins eBooks, appendices excluded).
claims.source: LotrProject, 'Word count and density' (via Wayback)
claims.quote: higher unique word density

claims.claim: Krege's 2000 German retranslation deliberately re-differentiated Tolkien's registers, modernising the hobbits' speech into late-1990s German against a biblical high style for Elves and human nobility, where Carroux (1969-70) had used one unified style.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: late 1990s German

claims.claim: German critics judged that Krege took too many liberties in a translator-centred approach unsuited to Tolkien, and the 2012 edition reverted the most controversial decisions.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: translator-centred approach

claims.claim: Linguist Rainer Nagel found that Krege corrects Carroux's errors but often overshoots his target.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: often overshoots its target

claims.claim: Carroux treated the source with enormous respect and a unified linguistic style, and Tolkien was delighted with her work apart from the poems.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: enormous respect

claims.claim: Krege's rendering of Sam's 'Master' as 'Chef' (boss) was criticised as misrepresenting a rural gardener's relation to his employer, and the September 2012 revision removed it.
claims.source: Der Herr der Ringe — Übersetzungen (de.wikipedia)
claims.quote: Chef

claims.claim: Krege spanned registers from sixteenth-century Bible German to colloquial speech but anchored them to 1990s German rather than the 1940s of the original, and many readers rejected the differentiation as overdrawn.
claims.source: Der Herr der Ringe — Übersetzungen (de.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Krege's 'unermüdlich wedelndem Laubwerk' for 'ever-moving leaves' was attacked for distorting the symbol of transience and Elvish departure.
claims.source: Der Herr der Ringe — Übersetzungen (de.wikipedia)
claims.quote: unermüdlich wedelndem Laubwerk

claims.claim: The German film dubbing kept Carroux's version rather than Krege's, visible in the third film's title remaining 'Die Rückkehr des Königs'.
claims.source: Der Herr der Ringe — Übersetzungen (de.wikipedia)
claims.quote: Die Rückkehr des Königs

claims.claim: Krege aimed to reproduce Tolkien's speech registers from Biblical language to 1940s British colloquialism, against what he saw as Carroux's uniform, artificially folksy German.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: highly disputed among fans

claims.claim: Krege's 1998 Hobbit restored the poems Scherf had cut but interpreted sentences freely and admitted anachronisms such as 'Hurricane'.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: Hurricane

claims.claim: Krege said he wanted to translate as Tolkien would write in 1999, directly from Westron into German.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Ardapedia)
claims.quote: directly from Westron to German

claims.claim: Krege's slang such as 'Penner' (bum) and 'Dalli Dalli' (hurry up) dated quickly and read as anachronistic.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Ardapedia)
claims.quote: Dalli Dalli

claims.claim: Krege replaced the historical deferential 'Ihr' with modern 'Sie', creating an odd modern formality in a medieval society.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Ardapedia)
claims.quote: Sie

claims.claim: Editor Ulrike Killer defended Krege's version as timely for the films and preferable to a monochromatic and dated Carroux.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Ardapedia)
claims.quote: monochromatic and dated

claims.claim: Lisa Kuppler's 2012 revision preserved Krege's stylistic approach but corrected orthography and restored the traditional address for Frodo.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Ardapedia)

claims.feature: translator's theory of colour and tempo
claims.claim: Krege (Tolkien Times, August 2000) set out to give the text its own life in the German language's room for 'Farbe, Tempo, Kontrasten'.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)
claims.quote: Farbe, Tempo, Kontrasten

claims.claim: Krege argued the old faithful translation inevitably makes the expression a little paler, the tempo slower and the style more uniform; Weinreich rejects 'paler' as nonsense but grants the rest.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)
claims.quote: ein wenig blasser, das Tempo langsamer

claims.claim: Weinreich argues 'Master' and 'Sir' express Sam's working-class standing against Frodo's gentry more than an employment relation, so Carroux's 'Herr' is correct and Krege's 'Chef' means what 'Boss' would mean, which is not in Tolkien.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)
claims.quote: das steht bei Tolkien aber nicht

claims.claim: In the Aglarond sentence Carroux keeps Tolkien's 'make ... bend' construction at some cost to fluency, while Krege's 'Kräuter' for 'weed' is botanically wrong where 'Wasserpflanzen' is right.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)
claims.quote: Kräuter

claims.feature: error density in a modernised text
claims.claim: A Deutsche Tolkien Gesellschaft project team found hundreds of smaller and larger errors in Krege's translation, which Weinreich attributes to a rush job ahead of the Jackson films.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)
claims.quote: hunderte kleinerer und größerer Fehler

claims.claim: Weinreich prefers Krege's 'Kunde' to Carroux's 'Bursche' for Farmer Maggot's 'fellow' (the Black Rider) because the modern word carries the original's ambivalence.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)
claims.quote: Kunde

claims.claim: Held's thesis finds Carroux foreignises through the archaic deferential 'Ihr' and at places awkward syntax, so that to a German reader her text may read like a translation from Middle High German.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)
claims.quote: at places awkward syntax

claims.claim: Krege uses modern German but preserves archaism where Tolkien contrasts archaic and modern speech, for example when Théoden first meets the hobbits at Isengard.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)

claims.claim: Krege's 'modern' words such as 'Halunke' no longer read as modern in 2021, while Nagel in 2004 objected to 'speziell' as ruining Butterbur's simple speech.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)
claims.quote: speziell

claims.claim: Nagel, quoted by Held, holds that Krege approached the book as a modernisation of Tolkien's text for what he believed was a new generation of readers.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)
claims.quote: a modernisation of Tolkien's text

claims.claim: Tolkien's Butterbur speaks an old-fashioned rural dialect; Krege gives him vernacular ('Dalli, dalli!' for 'Double sharp!') while Carroux translates verbatim ('Schneller, schneller!').
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)
claims.quote: Double sharp!

claims.claim: Krege repeatedly introduces German idioms where the English had none, turning Gandalf's 'I shall roast him' into 'wasch' ich ihm den Kopf' with oral contractions in a written letter, which loses the literal threat and alters Gandalf.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)
claims.quote: wasch' ich ihm den Kopf

claims.claim: Held concludes Krege is domesticating and dynamically equivalent while Carroux is foreignising and formally equivalent, so Krege's version shifts character perception more (Gollum and the Black Riders more or less animalistic, Galadriel's title and standing).
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)
