claims.quote: often minuscule

claims.claim: Both translations keep Tolkien's foreignised compound 'sister-son' as 'Schwestersohn' rather than 'Neffe'.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)
claims.quote: Schwestersohn

claims.claim: Nagel's chapter reports Krege defending his version as 'assimilating the alien' where Carroux merely rendered the text, and concludes that Krege's language for younger readers sometimes fails to convey the voice the author intended.
claims.source: Review: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Mythopoeic Society)
claims.quote: assimilating the alien

claims.claim: Honegger shows Tolkien's 'thou' carries five functions (poetry, archaism, contempt, emotion, familiarity) that German du/Sie and French tu/vous cannot reproduce.
claims.source: Review: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Mythopoeic Society)

claims.claim: Stenström notes the Swedish 'älvor' for elves imports unwanted fairy connotations.
claims.source: Review: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Mythopoeic Society)

claims.claim: Nagel's Prancing Pony example shows Krege shifting Butterbur from an elderly innkeeper to a younger colloquial speaker, e.g. 'Penner' where Carroux had 'Faultier'.
claims.source: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Cormarë 6) — Nagel and Honegger chapters (epdf mirror)
claims.quote: Penner

claims.claim: Nagel argues Krege's modernisation paradoxically creates a new uniformity by narrowing vocabulary range and simplifying archaic constructions.
claims.source: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Cormarë 6) — Nagel and Honegger chapters (epdf mirror)

claims.claim: Honegger explains that Tolkien equated Rohirric with Old English to keep linguistic distance while suggesting kinship, a choice translators cannot easily mirror.
claims.source: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Cormarë 6) — Nagel and Honegger chapters (epdf mirror)

claims.feature: reader verdict: register equated with ours
claims.claim: SpacePub readers objected that 'Chef' equates the hobbits' social circumstances with ours and that 'Penner', 'Imbissbude' and 'Stuss erzählen' break immersion, while supporters praised readability and regional differentiation of hobbit, Rohirric and Elvish speech.
claims.source: Der Herr der Ringe — die neue Übersetzung beurteilt (SpacePub forum archive)
claims.quote: Imbissbude

claims.claim: In the SF-Fan thread all twelve poll votes called the Krege translation an absolute failure, and one reader said the Middle-earth medieval atmosphere was gone, replaced by soap-opera modernity.
claims.source: Herr der Ringe — Krege-Übersetzung (SF-Fan forum)
claims.quote: die Stimmung ist nicht mehr die Mittelerde-Mittelalter-Atmosphäre

claims.claim: Literaturschock readers argued Tolkien's archaic language is used deliberately as a stylistic device, so modernisation destroys the novel, citing 'Chef' and an alleged 'beim Fundbüro' as anachronisms.
claims.source: Tolkiens Der Herr der Ringe — Carroux vs. Krege (Literaturschock forum)
claims.quote: altertümliche Sprache gezielt als Stilmittel verwendet wird

claims.claim: Redaktion42 holds that Carroux keeps elevated, formal dialogue across all characters while Krege's naturalistic hobbit speech brought jarring modern vocabulary, and that the 2012 edition struck out the first edition's sins.
claims.source: Welche Herr der Ringe-Übersetzung ist die beste? (redaktion42)
claims.quote: die Sünden der ersten Übersetzung herausgestrichen

claims.claim: The Deutsche Tolkien Gesellschaft states Carroux's translation is the more popular among many Tolkien fans, and Klett-Cotta reissued it in a 2019 boxed set.
claims.source: Drei Mal Carroux im Schuber (Deutsche Tolkien Gesellschaft)
claims.quote: bei vielen Tolkienfans die beliebtere

claims.claim: Twenty years after Krege the two translations still split German fans like almost no other topic, per the DTG's 2021 panel announcement.
claims.source: 20 Jahre nach Krege: Was taugen die deutschen Übersetzungen? (Deutsche Tolkien Gesellschaft)
claims.quote: spalten die Fans wie kaum ein anderes Thema

claims.claim: Krege criticised Carroux for using a similar linguistic style for the speech of both elves and hobbits despite the marked differences in the original.
claims.source: Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: similar linguistic style for the speech of both elves and hobbits

claims.claim: Domènech's Spanish rendered working-class hobbits in grammatically correct Spanish, losing Tolkien's double negatives, altered agreement and subject duplication.
claims.source: Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: grammatically correct Spanish

claims.claim: Tolkien's scheme maps Modern English to Westron, Old English to Rohirric and Old Norse to Dale, and Honegger suggests leaving Old English passages untranslated is probably best.
claims.source: Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: probably best

claims.feature: nomenclature not to be translated freely
claims.claim: Tolkien objected as strongly as possible to free translation of his nomenclature, writing the Guide after the Dutch and Swedish versions.
claims.source: Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: as strongly as is possible

claims.claim: Tolkien called Bilbo's wealth 'a legend' and Ohlmarks added that his travels were legendary too, an instance of embroidering every description.
claims.source: Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: propensity for embroidering every description

claims.claim: Tolkien's archaic fronting ('Weapons they have laid at your doors') cannot be done in French and is unmarked in German, so its archaic effect is lost in translation.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: Weapons they have laid at your doors

claims.claim: Gollum's non-standard syntax and plurals like 'pocketses' resist translation; Ledoux's French diminishes both Gollum's and the Gaffer's peculiarities.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: pocketses

claims.claim: Livnit's Hebrew used a high Biblical register, and Lottem's revision mixed in technical modern Hebrew to an odd result.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: odd result

claims.feature: register borrowed from a native genre
claims.claim: The Ding et al. Chinese version sounds like traditional wuxia fiction, while Chu produced a more popular version.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: sounds like traditional Chinese wuxia

claims.claim: Parcerisas deliberately larded his Catalan Hobbit with learned or slightly archaic forms for school readers, gave the southern Men (Boromir, Faramir) dialect traits, and made the orcs' speech as broken as possible.
claims.source: Francesc Parcerisas, 'Traduir J. R. R. Tolkien' (Traducció literària, URV 2018)
claims.quote: com més desballestat millor

claims.claim: Parcerisas notes the German case is the inverse of the Swedish: the first (Carroux) enjoys more prestige than the 2000 retranslation.
claims.source: Francesc Parcerisas, 'Traduir J. R. R. Tolkien' (Traducció literària, URV 2018)

claims.claim: Ohlmarks shifted Tolkien's simple language into hyperbolic, high-faluting expressions, adding words and long paraphrases throughout.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: high-faluting

claims.claim: Ohlmarks claimed he had produced an interpretation of Tolkien, not a straight translation, and refused revision.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: an interpretation of Tolkien, not a straight translation

claims.claim: Andersson's prose matched Tolkien's laconic tone, using 24 words where Ohlmarks used 42 in one sampled sentence.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Critics of the 2005 version called it readable, even and largely correct, with prose following the original's fluent style very closely.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: readable, even and in large part correct

claims.claim: Ohlmarks's interpretive names include Vattnadal (confusing 'riven' with 'river'), Lavskägge (reading 'beam' as light) and Björnavad (from 'Bruin').
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Tolkien found Ohlmarks a conceited person and his version even worse than the Dutch, and called the nine-page list of altered names both puzzling and irritating.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: a conceited person

claims.claim: One reviewer conceded Ohlmarks's 'Vidstige' even outdoes the original's 'Strider'.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: even outdoes the original's Strider

claims.claim: Tolkien's Guide to the Names was produced in response to Ohlmarks, and Ohlmarks later turned hostile, publishing Tolkien and Black Magic in 1982.
claims.source: Åke Ohlmarks (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Andreas Brunner (2004) wrote that Ohlmarks added adjectives and spruced up dialogue, producing a delightful but quite different book.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Leif Jacobsen documented padding such as 'six meals a day' becoming 'sex vällagade måltider om dagen'.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)
claims.quote: sex vällagade måltider om dagen

claims.claim: Ohlmarks stated in 1978 that he rewrote after a plain draft to make the world feel ancient and distant from England.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Malte Persson found the Ohlmarks text packed with misunderstandings, misreadings, inconsistencies and arbitrary additions, including Merry credited with the Witch-king's death-blow and two names for the Prancing Pony.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Henrik Williams argued Andersson's 'Min dyrgrip' for 'precious' is lexically correct but loses the corrupting allure that Ohlmarks's 'älskade' caught.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)
claims.quote: Min dyrgrip

claims.claim: Petter Lindgren expressed nostalgia for Ohlmarks's almost comically elaborate phrasing against Andersson's terse rendering.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Stefan Spjuth found 'Möcklegräva' for Michel Delving sounded like a place from Swedish MAD magazine.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Strömbom found the narrator's voice completely changed in the new translation, so that it was practically a question of two different works.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)
claims.quote: praktiskt taget var fråga om två olika verk

claims.claim: In the prologue's first sentence Tolkien and Andersson use simple language while Ohlmarks does not, turning 'a little' into 'en någorlunda klar bild av' against Andersson's 'litet'.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)
claims.quote: en någorlunda klar bild av

claims.claim: Ohlmarks's sentences are as a rule longer and more complex than the original's, with a somewhat higher stylistic value where Tolkien's word choice is simple and open.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)
claims.quote: något högre stilvalör

claims.claim: Ohlmarks turns 'the pale king' into 'den dödsbleke konungen' and 'bathed Frodo's shoulder' into a bathing 'med dekokten', consistently seeking more drama than the original.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)
claims.quote: den dödsbleke konungen

claims.claim: In 'Flight to the Ford' Ohlmarks's 'tröttnade aldrig på att inskärpa vikten av' adds a frenzy absent from Tolkien's and Andersson's matter-of-fact statements.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)
claims.quote: tröttnade aldrig på att inskärpa vikten av

claims.claim: Strömbom suggests Andersson sometimes cultivates a style even somewhat simpler than Tolkien's.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)
claims.quote: ännu något enklare än Tolkiens

claims.claim: The Tolkiens Arda reviewer holds that ornate language gets in the way of the story and that Andersson is more faithful to the English original than Ohlmarks, who added editorial glosses such as 'originell lustigkurre' at Bilbo's party.
claims.source: Recensionen: Ringarnas herre (Tolkiens Arda)
claims.quote: originell lustigkurre

claims.claim: Andersson said the heroic register, especially in Book V, was the hardest to translate, and that names allow no room to manoeuvre.
claims.source: Intervju: Erik Andersson — om Ringens brödraskap (Tolkiens Arda)
claims.quote: Det finns inget svängrum i ett namn

claims.claim: Andersson observed the book starts out as a children's book and moves into a more sinister mode, and that Aragorn's speech varies between ranger and king.
claims.source: Translating Tolkien — Erik Andersson interview (TheOneRing.net, 2004)
claims.quote: starts out as a children's book

claims.claim: Andersson called Ohlmarks's version excellent as a creation in its own right even if it does not always follow Tolkien.
claims.source: Translating Tolkien — Erik Andersson interview (TheOneRing.net, 2004)
claims.quote: As a creation in its own right it is excellent

claims.claim: The Tolkien på svenska essay charges that Andersson tones down the differences between the original's varieties of language, removes Sam's courteous address, lacks the ear for poetry, and that his small deviations all run in the same direction.
claims.source: Om Erik Anderssons översättning (Tolkien på svenska)
claims.quote: alla i samma riktning

claims.claim: The same essay insists that in Tolkien's text how something is said matters as much as what is said.
claims.source: Om Erik Anderssons översättning (Tolkien på svenska)

claims.claim: Johan Groth finds Andersson reduces 'pages', 'reader' and 'discover' to 'den', 'man' and 'få reda på', while Ohlmarks's showy style grows beyond all bounds.
claims.source: Ringarna herre (igen) samt några synpunkter på Åke Ohlmarks (Johan Groth)
claims.quote: prunkande stil

claims.claim: Andersson's diary records his fear of the 'anglicism ghost' and his search for names like 'Riftedal' that keep the English sound while reading as Swedish.
claims.source: Utdrag ur Översättarens anmärkningar (Erik Andersson diary excerpts)
claims.quote: anglicismspöket

claims.claim: Shippey's afterword considers Tolkien's imitators and what they do not imitate, notably language-building and interlaced storylines.
claims.source: T.A. Shippey — J.R.R. Tolkien: Author of the Century (Falling Letters review)

claims.claim: Shippey holds that no modern writer of fantasy has managed to escape the mark of Tolkien.
claims.source: J. R. R. Tolkien: Author of the Century (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: escape the mark of Tolkien

claims.claim: Shippey noted The Sword of Shannara's dogged adherence to Tolkien with point-for-point analogues (Sauron to Brona, Gandalf to Allanon, hobbits to Shea and Flick).
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: dogged

claims.claim: Lin Carter wrote that Brooks was not trying to imitate Tolkien's prose but to steal his story line and cast, calling it the most cold-blooded complete rip-off of another book.
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: wasn't trying to imitate Tolkien's prose

claims.claim: Brian Attebery called The Sword of Shannara undigested Tolkien with especially blatant correspondences, while Choice praised it as exceptionally well-written and very readable.
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: undigested Tolkien

claims.claim: Brooks acknowledged heavy Tolkien influence in his first novel and said he then adopted a popular-fiction approach rather than an academic tone.
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Contemporary critics of Shannara focused almost exclusively on plot and world-building parallels rather than prose, with Choice calling it exceptionally well-written.
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara: The Critics Fifty Years Later (Dark Worlds Quarterly)
claims.quote: exceptionally well-written, very readable

claims.claim: Vredenburgh judges that Shannara talks when it should at least be trying to sing, is bereft of atmosphere, and follows Tolkien's story architecture rather than his prose.
claims.source: Half a Century of Reading Tolkien, Part Seven: The Sword of Shannara (Black Gate)
claims.quote: talks when it should at least be trying to sing

claims.claim: Tom Simon finds Brooks's prose stilted and turgid, alternating between expository lumps and expository lumps feebly disguised as dialogue, with names uniformly slipshod.
claims.source: 1977: Lord of the Rinky-dink (Tom Simon, Bondwine)
claims.quote: expository lumps feebly disguised as dialogue

claims.claim: Simon cites Shippey's point that readers hungry for heroic fantasy would take any substitute no matter how diluted, and del Rey's targeting of young readers least likely to notice the writing.
claims.source: 1977: Lord of the Rinky-dink (Tom Simon, Bondwine)
claims.quote: take any substitute, no matter how diluted

claims.claim: The Big Bad Book Blog counts adjectives and adverbs at 21% of words in a sample passage, calls the prose wooden yet lightweight, and notes dialogue tags like 'blazed up angrily' replacing 'said'.
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara by Terry Brooks (The Big Bad Book Blog)
claims.quote: wooden yet lightweight

claims.claim: Dial H For Houston contrasts Tolkien's invented languages with Brooks naming a corner of the map after a direction, and calls the prose flat.
claims.source: Book Review: Terry Brooks' The Sword of Shannara (Dial H For Houston)
claims.quote: the prose is flat

claims.claim: Attebery said Shannara tries to evoke wonder without engaging the mind or emotions, reducing Tolkien to a bare formula; Jane Yolen saw derivative fantasy sinking into pastel unicorns and coy talking swords.
claims.source: Tolkien's impact on fantasy (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: pastel unicorns, coy talking swords

claims.claim: Critics stress that Tolkien's impression of depth and historical background is what formulaic followers fail to replicate.
claims.source: Tolkien's impact on fantasy (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: impression of depth

claims.claim: Le Guin characterised Tolkien's prose as quieter English of simple timelessness with sobriety, wit and force, ranging easily from the commonplace to the stately and able to slide into metrical poetry.
claims.source: It's intentional (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2011)
claims.quote: sobriety, wit and force

claims.claim: Tolkien defended Théoden's archaic speech on the ground that modern dialogue would create an insincerity of thought and a disunion of word and meaning, and gave Elrond the most archaisms as the eldest speaker.
claims.source: It's intentional (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2011)
claims.quote: a disunion of word and meaning

claims.claim: Le Guin faulted Zelazny and Leiber for talking colloquial American English when humour is intended and reverting to old formal usages at earnest moments.
claims.source: The Language of the Night by Ursula K Le Guin (Murray Ewing)
claims.quote: at earnest moments they revert to old formal usages

claims.claim: Le Guin's test is to change a passage's names to mundane ones and see whether it still reads as fantasy; Kurtz's Deryni fails as fancy dress.
claims.source: The Language of the Night by Ursula K Le Guin (Murray Ewing)
claims.quote: fancy dress

claims.claim: Le Guin warned against forced archaic language as a crutch, praising Tolkien's plain clear English, concrete vocabulary that avoids 'ichor', and the principle that the style is the book.
claims.source: From Elfland to Poughkeepsie to The Witcher (Nick Gibney)
claims.quote: ichor

claims.claim: Applying Le Guin, TheOneRing.net found The Rings of Power's 'Okay', 'like', 'Nah', 'Yeah' and 'conflicted' expose modern minds, while its over-correction lapses into fortune-cookie 'High Aphorism'.
claims.source: From The Rings of Power to Poughkeepsie (TheOneRing.net, 2022)
claims.quote: High Aphorism

claims.claim: Le Guin's essay separates the risky inner lands of Elfland from banal imitation that is the outside world in disguise, and Beagle called it the definitive piece on fantasy.
claims.source: From Elfland to Poughkeepsie (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: the definitive piece on fantasy

claims.claim: Brennan observes writers sticking '-st' on every second-person verb and '-th' on every third-person one, and warns archaic grammar is very easily overused.
claims.source: Archaic Grammar (Marie Brennan, Swan Tower)
claims.quote: very easily overused

claims.claim: Epic fantasy's archaisms fall into be-perfects ('Winter is come'), be- prefixes, hither/thither, thou/thee, postposed modifiers and do-less imperatives, used to suggest a whole past speech community.
claims.source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)
claims.quote: a whole past speech community

claims.claim: A commenter notes the Nazgûl uses thee/thou while Éowyn answers in modern 'you', and that Tolkien was very deliberate about when he used 'thou'.
claims.source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)
claims.quote: very deliberate about when he used 'thou'

claims.claim: 'From whence it came' is a common archaism error because 'whence' already contains 'from'.
claims.source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)
claims.quote: from whence

claims.claim: Bored of the Rings steps through the prologue, the map and the main text in turn, substituting brand names (Moxie and Pepsi, Serutan) for Tolkien's invented terms.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The parody replaces Tolkien's Sindarin hymn with nonsense modern references ('Unicef clearasil') and parodies the Watcher in the Water as a thesaurus-monster.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: Unicef clearasil

claims.claim: David Bratman remarked that the parodists wrought better than they knew, since Tolkien's drafts came close to writing the parody version of his own novel before he avoided it.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: wrought better than they knew

claims.claim: David Barnett judged the parody shows respect and affection for the source despite its crudity.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The Phuulish Fellow review finds the parody works best when it references Tolkien's own recognisable words and phrases, includes copious inserted verse, and that Tolkien's Party speech is actually funnier than the parody.
claims.source: Review: Bored of the Rings (1969) (A Phuulish Fellow)
claims.quote: actually funnier than the parody

claims.claim: My Tolkien Archive judges the parody mimics the forms (foreword, map, prologue) with lazy names, without genuine engagement with Tolkien's prose itself.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings: A Parody (My Tolkien Archive)

claims.claim: Pechey Ponderings notes the parody's embedded songs are well-crafted and its foreword disclaims any attempt to fill Tolkien's shoes.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings review (Pechey Ponderings)

claims.claim: The Tough Guide's Stew entry mocks stew as the universal fantasy meal even though it takes forty times as long to prepare as steak.
claims.source: The DWJ Project: Tough Guide to Fantasyland (Swan Tower)
claims.quote: forty times as long to prepare as steak

claims.claim: The Guide observes that few Fantasyland names are considered complete unless interrupted by an apostrophe nobody knows how to pronounce.
claims.source: The Tough Guide To Fantasyland — Review (HearWriteNow)
claims.quote: complete unless interrupted by an apostrophe

claims.claim: Shalizi's review frames the Guide as an attack on fifty years of trilogies that are debased versions of The Lord of the Rings, which Jones calls elf operas.
claims.source: Diana Wynne Jones, The Tough Guide to Fantasyland (Cosma Shalizi review)
claims.quote: elf operas

claims.claim: The English Student review reads entries from 'Stew' to 'Reek of Wrongness' as exposing a tour of something made just strange enough to fascinate, with Tolkien as the deeply English conservative template.
claims.source: Review: The Tough Guide to Fantasyland (The English Student)
claims.quote: made just strange enough to fascinate

claims.claim: Wikipedia describes the Guide's tone as either thinly veiled criticism of the genre's derivative nature or an affectionate study.
claims.source: The Tough Guide to Fantasyland (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: thinly veiled criticism

claims.claim: Sibley and Bakewell's script incorporated many sections of dialogue lifted directly from the book, such as the Window on the West conversations.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: many sections of dialogue lifted directly

claims.claim: Sibley preferred removing minor characters entirely to the alternative, which would have been to fabricate dialogue for them.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: to fabricate dialogue for them

claims.claim: The adaptation radically restructured books 3-6, flattening Tolkien's interlacing into the Appendix chronology and splicing Frodo and Sam's journey with events in the West.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Christopher Tolkien approved the scripts and recorded a cassette of correct pronunciations of Middle-earth names for the cast.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Rosebury praised the dialogue delivery and Woodthorpe's Gollum but found the skilful abridgement subtly reshaped Tolkien's text in the direction of an adventure story.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: in the direction of an adventure story

claims.claim: Christina Scull called it a masterly adaptation that caught the spirit of the books, found the alliterative-verse handling of the Pelennor a brilliant idea, and contrasted its characters as in the book with the films' weakening of almost all the characters.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: a brilliant idea

claims.claim: The Tolkien Library review states Tolkien's language is left intact in the mouths of the proper characters, delivered with highly trained diction that keeps the subtle differences in accents of the book.
claims.source: Review: The BBC Lord of the Rings Dramatization (Tolkien Library)
claims.quote: left intact in the mouths of the proper characters

claims.claim: The production set many poems to music, with Bill Nighy singing the fall of Gil-galad and Bilbo's Last Song and Douglas Livingstone reciting the Khazad-dûm poem.
claims.source: Review: The BBC Lord of the Rings Dramatization (Tolkien Library)

claims.claim: Brunstrom hears Robert Stephens's Prancing-Pony rusticity remain a leitmotif against his later kingly majesty, and notes Sibley keeps as much of Tolkien's dialogue as possible.
claims.source: The 1981 BBC Lord of the Rings radio adaptation reviewed (Conrad Brunstrom)
claims.quote: remains a leitmotif

claims.claim: To spare the narrator, descriptions were transferred into dialogue, so that Sam is awkwardly forced to narrate his Shelob fight in real time.
claims.source: The 1981 BBC Lord of the Rings radio adaptation reviewed (Conrad Brunstrom)
claims.quote: awkwardly forced to narrate

claims.claim: The Pelennor Fields sequence interweaves battle dialogue between verses of a Rohan lay written afterwards.
claims.source: The 1981 BBC Lord of the Rings radio adaptation reviewed (Conrad Brunstrom)

claims.claim: Brundige reports Sibley and Bakewell use Tolkien's words almost exclusively except for stage directions, and shun flashback and the narrator's voice as much as possible.
claims.source: The BBC Radio Play of LOTR — a Fan's Review (Ellen Brundige, istad.org)
claims.quote: use Tolkien's words almost exclusively

claims.claim: For the Pelennor the adapters combed Tolkien's prose and recast lines of it in metre and alliteration as extra ballad stanzas, e.g. 'crashed to the ground with the king crushed beneath him'.
claims.source: The BBC Radio Play of LOTR — a Fan's Review (Ellen Brundige, istad.org)
claims.quote: with the king crushed beneath him

claims.claim: Brundige praises a Faramir whose courtly speech shows his quality and an Aragorn whose manner of speech is altered not a jot, as proof that Tolkien's heroes can sound like flesh-and-blood people.
claims.source: The BBC Radio Play of LOTR — a Fan's Review (Ellen Brundige, istad.org)
claims.quote: manner of speech altered not a jot

claims.claim: Brundige argues that language is part of what makes the book stand out and radio gives it full wings to fly.
claims.source: The BBC Radio Play of LOTR — a Fan's Review (Ellen Brundige, istad.org)
claims.quote: radio gives it full wings to fly

claims.claim: Sibley (2019) said he used a narrator because it lets you capture the authorial voice of the book, convey place and passing time, and move across scenes when the Fellowship splits.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: capture the authorial voice of the book

claims.claim: Contains Moderate Peril notes great care was taken with pronunciation and with dialogue spoken in Elvish and the Black Speech, and that characterisations and dialogue were extremely well realised.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings — BBC Radio Adaptation (1981) (Contains Moderate Peril)
claims.quote: the delivery of dialogue spoken in Elvish

claims.claim: Sibley's own page credits Gerard Murphy with the series' strong narrative voice, notes Christopher Tolkien's pronunciation cassette, and concedes that Tolkien's interlaced chronology could not be applied to a dramatic presentation.
claims.source: Brian Sibley: The Works — The Lord of the Rings (BBC Radio 1981)

claims.claim: Tolkien told Tiller in 1956 that dramatisation results in too great an emphasis on dialogue, mostly with its setting removed.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1955 radio series) (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: too great an emphasis on dialogue

claims.claim: In 1957 Tolkien wrote he would find vulgarisation less painful than the sillification achieved by the BBC.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1955 radio series) (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: sillification

claims.claim: Series One, which cut scenes, was welcomed (appreciation 64/100); Series Two, which compressed them, was heard as a footling and ridiculous-sounding adventure story.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1955 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.feature: dialogue preserved as far as possible
claims.claim: Tiller promised Tolkien that the dialogue of the original book would be preserved as far as possible, with a narrator linking scenes and cutting preferred to summarising.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: preserved as far as possible

claims.claim: Tiller admitted that a great deal of the flavour of the work had been lost through telescoping incidents, and Tolkien replied he did not think more could have been done in the time.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: a great deal of the flavour

claims.claim: Tolkien rejected the expectation that hobbits should pipe and squeak, asking why tones should rise with fall in stature, and judged the Elves managed excellently, the Council of Elrond masterly, and Bilbo bored.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: Why should tones rise with fall in stature?

claims.claim: Tolkien liked Glóin's accent but found it heavily laid on, noting dwarves spoke the Common Tongue natively with a uvular back R.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: heavily laid on

claims.claim: A 1955 review held that Tolkien's relaxed, vivid and masculine style with its rich coinages adapted naturally to radio and held attention even when expository.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: relaxed, vivid, and masculine style

claims.claim: Listeners to the compressed Series Two called it an absolute ruin and a farce whose ignominious compression produced a juvenile adventure story.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story

claims.claim: Tolkien described Norman Shelley's Bombadil as dreadful and the announcer's misdescription of Goldberry and Willowman as worse still (Letters 175, 176, 198).
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: dreadful

claims.claim: The 1979 Mind's Eye version removed much back history and expository narration and, with lines recorded separately, produced curiously stilted exchanges of dialogue and frequent mispronunciations.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings — The Mind's Eye Radio Adaptation (1979) (Contains Moderate Peril)
claims.quote: curiously stilted exchanges of dialogue

claims.claim: Wikipedia notes the Virginia theatre players of the 1979 adaptation had difficulty pronouncing the names of characters and places, though the version kept Tom Bombadil.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1979 radio series) (Wikipedia)

The words 'a Secondary World' are the claim's gloss for Tolkien's 'ideal creations'/Sub-creation, which the essay uses interchangeably.

541.note: Same PDF. Quote verbatim: 'The moment disbelief arises, the spell is broken; the magic, or rather art, has failed.' Nowhere does the page prescribe that words must sound like what they mean; that limb is the claim's own gloss.

'in language-making' is context-supported: the sentence sits in the essay on invented languages and the next sentence applies it to Naffarin, his own construction.

561.note: Raw PDF (22pp, pypdf). Quote verbatim: 'The illusion of historical truth and perspective, that has made Beowulf seem such an attractive quarry, is largely a product of art.' 562.trueWording: impression of depth... episodes and allusions, mostly darker than the foreground
562.note: Quote verbatim: 'This impression of depth is an effect and a justification of the use of episodes and allusions to old tales, mostly darker, more pagan, and desperate than the foreground.' The closing gloss 'the background must be grimmer than the story' is a normative restatement of the same sentence, and Tolkien's own 'effect and a justification' framing licenses it.

563.note: Quote verbatim, and the whole allegory is on the page: 'A man inherited a field in which was an accumulation of old stone, part of an older hall... Of the rest he took some and built a tower... So they pushed the tower over' to look for carvings, another 'began to dig' for coal 'and forgot even the stones' — 'But from the top of that tower the man had been able to look out upon the sea.' 822.note: Wikipedia: 'The Tolkien scholar David Bratman, writing in Mythlore, quotes an extended passage... commenting "Those parodists wrought better than they knew". He explains that Tolkien, in his many drafts, came very close to "inadvertently writing the parody version of his own novel", though in the end he managed to avoid that, in Bratman's view, remarkably completely.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

823.trueWording: respect and affection for the source material shines through
823.note: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bored_of_the_Rings fetched as raw wikitext (Special:Export). Reception para: Barnett finds it 'very funny, albeit perhaps less sophisticated than more modern parodies. But Kenney and Beard's respect and affection for the source material shines through.' Crudity limb also on page: the book 'sits somewhere between ... Mad and ... Animal House - cruder than the former but not quite as rude as the latter.' Claim carried no quote string, so substance grade.

824.note: phuulishfellow.wordpress.com raw page. Quote 'actually funnier than the parody' appears word for word: 'Birthday Party Farewell Speech - Tolkien's version is actually funnier than the parody.' Limb 1: 'The earlier sections ... go so far as to reference Tolkien's own recognisable words and phrases, are much stronger.' Limb 2: 'there are copious inserted poems and songs, after the manner of Tolkien.' All limbs supported.

825.trueWording: spends a lot of time imitating the forms of it
825.note: mytolkienarchive.wordpress.com raw page. Supported: 'It certainly spends a lot of time imitating the forms of it' (cover art, the authors' statement mimicking Tolkien's Ace-paperback response, 'to the maps, the most basic story and overall shape of things') and the lazy-names limb ('Dildo Buggers! Really? That's the best you could come up with? ... Lazy.'). NOT supported: the review never discusses Tolkien's prose; its complaint is absence of affection/appreciation ('it never really feels like there's any affection there'; 'any hint that they actually appreciate the original work as anything other than a platform'). 'Foreword' appears nowhere on the page; 'prologue' appears only inside the page's blockquoted Wikipedia summary, not in the reviewer's own judgement.
825.unsupportedLimb: no genuine engagement with Tolkien's prose itself - the review never mentions prose (its charge is lack of affection); 'foreword' is absent from the page and 'prologue' occurs only in the quoted Wikipedia blurb

826.trueWording: the songs that are embedded throughout ... were well-crafted
826.note: pecheyponderings.wordpress.com raw page. Songs limb: 'from the various creatures that Frito encounters through to the songs that are embedded throughout. I can admit that these were well-crafted.' Disclaimer limb: 'Beard and Kenney open with the admission that they are not trying to fill the shoes that Tolkien left, but prefer to write something satirical for their own amusement.' The page says they 'open with the admission' rather than naming a foreword; claim carried no quote string, so substance grade.

827.note: swantower.com raw page. Quote 'forty times as long to prepare as steak' appears word for word, inside the Tough Guide's STEW entry as quoted in the thread by the blog's own author (Marie Brennan): 'Stew ... is the staple FOOD in Fantasyland ... Stew will be what you are served to eat every single time ... it takes forty times as long to prepare as steak.' Universal-meal limb supported by 'staple FOOD' + 'every single time'. Note the quotation sits in the post's comment thread, not the post body.

828.trueWording: complete unless they are interrupted by an apostrophe
828.note: hearwritenow.com raw page. Entry quoted in full: 'Apostrophes: Few names in Fantasyland are considered complete unless they are interrupted by an apostrophe somewhere in the middle... No one knows the reasons for this. Nor does anyone really know how an apostrophe should be pronounced...' Every limb supported, but the claim's quote string drops 'they are', so it is not word for word - substance, not verbatim.

829.trueWording: 'elf operas,' as they were recently named on Usenet
829.note: bactra.org raw page. Quote 'elf operas' present, and the fifty-years/debased-trilogies limb is verbatim: 'it is still, fifty years on, churning out trilogies which are debased versions of The Lord of the Rings --- ``elf operas,'' as they were recently named on Usenet.' But Shalizi credits the coinage to Usenet, not to Jones; Jones is credited only with 'an open, flagrant and ... hilarious parody'.
829.unsupportedLimb: which Jones calls elf operas - Shalizi attributes the term to Usenet ('as they were recently named on Usenet'), not to Jones

830.note: englishstudens.com raw page. Quote 'made just strange enough to fascinate' word for word: 'a tour of something made just strange enough to fascinate, in an othering kind of way'. Entry range limb: 'Entries range from Stew ... through Goddesses and Gods ... to Reek of Wrongness'. Tolkien limb: 'it's Tolkien, a deeply English and deeply conservative writer, whose work has become the model for the genre'.

831.note: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tough_Guide_to_Fantasyland fetched as raw wikitext. Description section: 'It can all be read as a thinly veiled criticism of the fantasy genre as overly derivative, cliched, and unimaginative. Alternatively it can be seen as an affectionate study of the themes and ideas that resonate through fantasy writing.' Quote verbatim; both alternatives supported. Framing note: the article says the book 'can all be read as' this, and treats 'tone' in the next sentence ('The tone is generally tongue-in-cheek') - the either/or is intact either way.

832.note: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lord_of_the_Rings_(1981_radio_series) raw wikitext. Development>Writing: 'The script attempts to be as faithful as possible to the original novel with many sections of dialogue lifted directly from the source material, such as the conversations between Frodo, Sam and Faramir in “The Window on the West”.' Quote verbatim; all limbs supported. (Claim's page locator says 'Production'; the live article's section is Development > Writing.)

833.note: Same article, Development>Writing: 'On the decision to excise some minor characters who appeared for only a few lines of the book, Sibley stated he felt it preferable to remove the character altogether than the alternative, “which would have been to fabricate dialogue for them.”' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

834.trueWording: flattening out Tolkien's interlacing by splicing Frodo and Sam with the West
834.note: Same article, Development>Writing: 'The adaptation radically restructured the chronology of the chapters in Books 3-6, flattening out Tolkien's interlacing by splicing the journey of Frodo and Sam with events in the West. This aligned them with the timeline of events provided by Tolkien in the Appendices.' Every limb supported; claim carried no quote string, so substance grade.

835.trueWording: reviewed and approved the final scripts; recorded a pronunciation cassette
835.note: Same article, Development>Writing: 'The author's son and editor Christopher Tolkien reviewed and approved the final scripts for each episode. He recorded an audio cassette of correct pronunciations for Middle-earth words and names to assist the cast during recordings.' Both limbs supported; claim carried no quote string, so substance grade.

836.note: Same article, Analysis section: 'He finds the dialogue well delivered by the actors, admiring especially Peter Woodthorpe's “fine Gollum”, and the abridgement skilful though subtly flattening Tolkien's text “in the direction of an adventure story.”' Quote verbatim; every limb supported (claim's 'reshaped' = page's 'flattening'). Claim's page locator says 'Reception'; the section is titled Analysis.

837.note: Same article, Analysis section: Scull 'thought it a “masterly adaptation” ... especially “caught the spirit of the books”. She found the handling of the Battle of the Pelennor Fields with alliterative verse “a brilliant idea” ... disliking the films' additional material, violence, and “the weakening of almost all the characters” ... the BBC dramatisation presented “the characters I [met] in the book”.' Quote 'a brilliant idea' verbatim; all four limbs supported. Section is Analysis, not Reception.

838.note: Collier: 'tolkien's language is left intact in the mouths of the proper characters'; separately 'still highly trained in diction ... while still retaining all subtle differences in accents', and 'subtle varieties in accents, which one also finds in the books'. Every limb on the raw page.

839.trueWording: Nighy sings Gil-galad; Le Mesurier sings Bilbo's Last Song
839.note: Verified: 'putting many of the poems and songs to music'; 'William Nighy as Sam singing a part of the fall of Gil-Galad'; 'Douglas Livingstone does a splendid job with Gimli's Khazad-dum poem'. But the page attributes Bilbo's Last Song to John Le Mesurier ('a demo version of John Le Mesurier singing Bilbo's Last Song'); its own sentence names Nighy's second song as 'his song in the tower of Minas Morgul', not Bilbo's Last Song.
839.unsupportedLimb: that Bill Nighy sings Bilbo's Last Song - the page credits John Le Mesurier

840.note: Brunstrom: 'the rusticity of Strider remains a leitmotif that interrupts the steady majesty of King Elessar', after 'When you hear him for the first time in the Prancing Pony, he sounds rustic'; and 'His dramatisation keeps as much of Tolkien's dialogue as possible.' Quoted phrase 'remains a leitmotif' word for word.

841.note: Brunstrom: 'a tendency not to want to work the narrator (Gerard Murphy) too hard, and to attempt to transfer some of the descriptions into dialogue'; 'Sam (Bill Nighy) is rather awkwardly forced to narrate the process of his battle with Shelob in real time.' Quoted phrase present verbatim.

842.trueWording: singing the Rohan lay written in its wake, battle dialogue between verses
842.note: Brunstrom: 'The Battle of the Pelennor Fields is developed cleverly by singing the Rohan lay written in its wake and inserting battle dialogue in between its verses.' Claim carries no quote field; 'written afterwards' is the page's 'written in its wake' in other words, hence SUBSTANCE not VERBATIM.

843.note: Brundige, Appendix A: 'Sibley and Bakewell use Tolkien's words almost exclusively, except for stage directions (e.g. Frodo exclaiming, "the river is rising!")'; 'The radio play shuns flashback and the narrator's voice as much as possible.' Both limbs and the quote on the raw page; page label 'Appendix A' correct.

844.note: Brundige: 'Sibley and Bakewell meticulously combed through Tolkien's narrative of the battle and adapted lines of its description, in meter, with appropriate alliteration ... lines had been added ... which in fact were not originally part of these songs'; the example 'crashed to the ground with the king crushed beneath him' appears verbatim, and narrative there 'is provided by stanzas of the ballad'.

845.note: Brundige: 'a Faramir whose voice and courtly speech "show his quality" as much as his deeds: proof that one can capture Tolkien's larger-than-life heroes faithfully yet have them sound like flesh-and-blood people. Aragorn, too, is both human and hero, his manner of speech altered not a jot.' Quote verbatim.

846.note: Brundige: 'Language is part of what makes the Lord of the Rings stand out, and radio gives it full wings to fly.' Quoted phrase word for word.

847.note: Lee PDF (fetched as binary, text extracted with pypdf), footnote 7: Sibley 'used one in 1981 (Gerard Murphy) as it allowed you to "capture the authorial voice of the book", convey a sense of place and passing of time, move you across scenes (especially useful when the Fellowship splits up)', cited '(Sibley, 2019)'. Every limb, in footnote 7 as claimed.

848.note: Roger Edwards: 'Great care was taken with pronunciation of words and the delivery of dialogue spoken in Elvish and the Black Speech.' and 'The characterisations and dialogue were extremely well realised'. Quote verbatim; the fetched page is the 24 Nov post itself, not a snippet.

849.trueWording: Tolkien wanted the threads NOT interwoven but on individual chronology
849.note: Verified on Sibley's blog: 'Gerard Murphy, who gave the series its strong narrative voice'; Christopher Tolkien's help 'included recording an audiocassette of the acceptable pronunciation of Middle-earth words and names'. But the chronology sentence reads: Tolkien 'had been adamant that the two main threads ... should not be interwoven, but should follow their own individual chronology, as they do in the book', which Sibley concluded could not 'be applied to a dramatic presentation'. The page's word is un-interwoven/individual, the opposite of the claim's 'interlaced'.
849.unsupportedLimb: calling the chronology Sibley rejected 'interlaced' - the page says Tolkien insisted the threads NOT be interwoven, each on its own chronology

850.note: Wikipedia quotes Tolkien to Tiller, November 1956: 'it requires rather the older art of the reading "mime", than the more nearly dramatic, which results in too great an emphasis on dialogue (mostly with its setting removed)'. Quote verbatim; date and addressee both on the page (ref #194 to Terence Tiller, 6 November 1956).

851.note: Wikipedia: 'Replying to Rayner Unwin in 1957 ... he wrote: "I think I should find vulgarization less painful than the sillification achieved by the B.B.C."' Quoted word 'sillification' verbatim; year and sense exact (page spells vulgarization with a z).

852.trueWording: first series welcomed, 64/100 by last episode; second compressed, criticised
852.note: Wikipedia: 'audience appreciation had by the last episode reached 64 out of 100 from an initial score of 56'; listeners 'enjoyed the first series, where Tiller had followed Tolkien's advice to make a selection of scenes and cut the rest. They were far more critical of the second series, where Tiller had compressed many scenes, resulting in what a self-described "Civil Servant" called "a footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story"'. Two caveats short of VERBATIM: 64 is the last-episode score (initial 56), and the footling phrase is one named listener's, quoted by the page as the result of the compression, not a general verdict.
852.unsupportedLimb: the general verdict - 'a footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story' is one named listener's phrase, quoted as the result of the compression

853.trueWording: Tiller: 'the dialogue of the original book would be preserved as far as possible'
853.note: Lee, p.2: Tiller's 2/2/55 reply carries the quote verbatim; 'A Narrator would be used to link scenes'; 'Cutting would be necessary... but he preferred this to excessive summarising'. Every limb on the raw PDF text.

854.trueWording: 'inevitably a great deal of the flavour of your work has been lost'
854.note: Raw PDF: Tiller 21/9/55 quote verbatim, then 'Tiller had therefore telescope[d] incidents'; Tolkien 27/9/55: 'I do not think that with the time at your disposal you could have done any better'.

855.trueWording: 'Why should tones rise with fall in stature?'
855.note: Raw PDF: quote verbatim; same sentence carries Hobbits should 'pipe and squeak', Elves 'managed excellently', Council of Elrond 'masterly', Bilbo sounded 'bored'. All five limbs present.

856.trueWording: 'heavily laid on'; 'dwarves spoke the Common Tongue natively... uvular back R'
856.note: Raw PDF: 'He liked Gloin's accent but added it was a bit heavily laid on noting dwarves spoke the Common Tongue natively, like Jews, but they had a uvular back R'. Claim omits 'like Jews' but adds nothing unsupported.

857.trueWording: 'relaxed, vivid, and masculine style with its rich coinages'
857.note: Raw PDF: uncatalogued clipping review 'The Meaning of the Ring' 15/11/55 (so 1955); 'adapted naturally to radio'; 'holds the attention even when he is being expository'.

858.note: Raw PDF: all four phrases in one sentence about Series Two; the claim's quote field 'footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story' is also verbatim in the following Civil Servant listener comment.

859.note: Raw PDF footnote 2: Letters #175 (Molly Waldron 30/11/55) carries both quotes; the same footnote cites Letters #176 and #198. Note: #176/#198 are cited as further references, not as the source of the two quoted phrases.
859.unsupportedLimb: the citation of Letters #176 and #198, which are cited on the page as further references, not as the source of the two quoted phrases

860.trueWording: 'some curiously stilted exchanges of dialogue in key scenes'
860.note: Raw page: 'much of the back history, lore and expositionary narration removed'; 'the cast often recorded their lines separately resulting in some curiously stilted exchanges'; 'The pronunciation of many names and places are often incorrect'.

861.trueWording: 'had difficulty pronouncing the names of characters and places'
861.note: Raw Wikipedia text: that phrase is word for word (attributed there to the SF-Worlds review of the local Virginia theater players); the article separately says it is 'notable for including the Tom Bombadil scenes'.

862.trueWording: Post says Jackson uses accents 'immersing them in the sounds'
862.note: Register limbs all verbatim: Appendix F 'hobbits indeed spoke for the most part a rustic dialect, whereas in Gondor and Rohan a more antique language was used'; 'Jackson uses accents to convey these differences instead'; the conditional-syntax contrast and the film line 'The Ring is altogether evil' are both on the page (dated April 11, 2017).
862.unsupportedLimb: Accents called 'visual' - the post treats accents as auditory ('immersing them in the sounds of Middle Earth'), explicitly distinct from the films' visuals

863.trueWording: Tolkien 'never operates on an ironic level'; 'verse is very rarely present'
863.note: Raw page: movies 'take multiple breaks to laugh at characters, mainly Merry, Pippin, or Gimli'; 'Tolkien never poked direct fun at the characters'; poems 'distinguish the different races of Middle Earth' yet verse is very rarely present in Jackson. Claim is paraphrase, not quotation (empty quote field).

864.trueWording: Croft argues both men 'flatten[ed]' Tolkien's characters, dialogue, and plot
864.note: Raw Wikipedia text of the Mithril Coats and Tin Ears row: 'both men' = Jackson and Morton Zimmerman; 'too much too soon' is supported by 'where Tolkien subtly builds tension, Jackson habit[ually] gives away what will happen' and the essay's 'Anticipation'. The page renders the quoted word with a bracketed inflection, 'flatten[ed]'.

865.trueWording: Gollum's 'extraordinary idiolect' is Rosebury's phrase, not theirs
865.note: The Fellowship table 'after Kullmann and Siepmann' supports five limbs exactly: Aragorn Archaic/literary with Inversion; Sam Colloquial, rustic, working class, 'Often politely hedged'; Gandalf Plain, flexible, Commands; Gimli and Legolas Literary with Proverbs. Kullmann and Siepmann's corpus linguistics is also stated. But Gollum is outside the table and outside their attribution.
865.unsupportedLimb: Gollum's idiolect of obsessive repetition and minimal syntax - the page attributes that to Brian Rosebury; Kullmann and Siepmann are cited only for Gollum's 'non-standard speech'

866.trueWording: 'only a few actually archaic words'; 'nostalgic, maybe even archaic'
866.note: Raw Wikipedia text, Syntax and diction: Walker on 'only a few actually archaic words'; diction 'manages to seem in its essence nostalgic, maybe even archaic'; and antiquity coming from 'deem', 'moot', 'wight' combined with still-current 'darkling' and 'westering'.

867.trueWording: readers experience it as 'an impression of exalted register'
867.note: Raw Wikipedia text: Turner on the Pelennor eucatastrophe passage - paratactic style with repeated 'and' 'in the manner of the New Testament', the impression arising 'because of the biblical association'; Turner's 'special stylistic effects at key moments' supports the key-moments limb. The page says Tolkien uses 'few unusual or archaic words' there rather than none.
867.unsupportedLimb: 'no archaic words' - the page says Tolkien uses 'few unusual or archaic words' in the passage, not none

868.trueWording: "the clipped language of army dispatches" (Vaninskaya, quoted verbatim)
868.note: Raw wikitext of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolkien's_prose_style fetched with a browser UA via ?action=raw. Section 'Varied dialogue types for the enemy': 'Anna Vaninskaya writes that the most modern idiom in The Lord of the Rings is used by the Orcs overheard by Frodo and Sam in Mordor. Tolkien gives them the speech of the twentieth century, whether as soldiers, functionaries in party or government, or "minor officials in a murderous bureaucracy".' Two sentences later: 'She writes that Tolkien captures, too, "the clipped language of army dispatches"'. Every limb supported: Vaninskaya as attributor, most-modern-idiom, Orcs, army dispatches, bureaucrats.

869.trueWording: goes furthest with Riders of Rohan; words 'rescued from total obscurity'
869.note: No quotation supplied in the claim, so graded on substance; the page nevertheless carries the claim's distinctive words verbatim. Section 'Incorporating the archaic, even Old English': 'Tolkien goes furthest with the Riders of Rohan, giving them "Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns" ... He gives Rohan speakers words "rescued from total obscurity" like "éored", Old English for "a troop of cavalry", "dwimmerlaik", and "mearas".' The actual-phrases limb: 'Finally, Tolkien has his Riders of Rohan speak a few phrases directly in Old English, as when Éomer shouts "Westu Théoden hál!"'. All three limbs supported.

870.trueWording: "more rarefied air" (Shippey, quoted verbatim on the page)
870.note: Section 'The Silmarillion': 'The Silmarillion, by contrast with The Lord of the Rings, is written in a compressed style, in which events are briefly documented as if in annals recording history and legend, rather than described with much focus on persons or the niceties of conventional storytelling' (attributed to Bratman); the next sentence: 'Shippey states that The Silmarillion comes across to the reader as a more distant and mythic work ... there was in his view no place for humorously earthy Hobbits in the "more rarefied air" of that work.' Quote verbatim and both factual limbs present; the claim's connective 'giving' joins two adjacent, same-subject sentences by different scholars (Bratman for the annals limb, Shippey for the phrase) rather than reproducing a stated causal link.
870.unsupportedLimb: the causal connective 'giving' - the page joins two adjacent sentences by different scholars (Bratman for the annals, Shippey for 'more rarefied air') without asserting the link

871.trueWording: some 45 to 50 stories, 23 characters, about half dialogue, 85% Hobbit
871.note: No quotation supplied, so graded on substance; all three figures match exactly. Section 'Narrative quality': 'There are some 45 to 50 stories embedded in the text of The Lord of the Rings, supposedly narrated by 23 of the novel's characters. ... About half of The Lord of the Rings consists of dialogue, poetry, or stories told by a character. The other half is narrative, often from the point of view of one of the characters, and usually – 85% of the time – a Hobbit protagonist.' (Kullmann and Siepmann). The 85% is of the narrative half specifically, which is what the claim says.

872.unsupportedLimb: that Rosebury refuted Moorcock's charge — the page ties Rosebury's reply only to Stimpson's attack, never to Moorcock
872.trueWording: Rosebury 'systematically replies to each item in Stimpson's attack'
872.note: Quote verbatim and the two accusations are exact. Lead and 'Criticism' section: Stimpson 'wrote in 1969 that Tolkien not only "shun[s] ordinary diction, he also wrenches syntax"'; 'In 1978 ... Michael Moorcock, in his essay Epic Pooh, criticized Tolkien for utilizing a comforting and unchallenging writing style'. Rosebury limb: 'The scholar of humanities Brian Rosebury systematically replies to each item in Stimpson's attack, showing that Tolkien mostly uses plain modern English.' The page confines Rosebury's rebuttal to Stimpson; the claim's plural 'charges Rosebury refuted' extends it to Moorcock, which the page does not support. Note also the page says 'mostly uses plain modern English'.

873.trueWording: "familiar phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off'" vs "'wear' and 'dismount'"
873.note: Raw wikitext of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolkien:_A_Cultural_Phenomenon fetched with a browser UA via ?action=raw. Reception section: 'Allan Turner comments in the same work that Rosebury rejects the unsupported assertions of archaising and "wrenched syntax" by critics like Catharine Stimpson, and that Rosebury pointed out that Tolkien used a plain descriptive style, demonstrably favouring the "familiar phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off' .. to the slightly more literary 'wear' and 'dismount'".' Quote verbatim; every limb supported. Only difference is intensity: the page reads 'slightly more literary', the claim 'the more literary'.
873.unsupportedLimb: the dropped hedge - the page reads 'slightly more literary', not 'the more literary'
